All grammar

N5 Grammar

です / だ

Politeです
Casualだ

Same meaning: "is". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 5

あ、いいえ試作品です

"Oh, no, [it's] a prototype."

です says what something is, the polite way. It goes right after a noun (and after な-adjectives, covered later): thing + です = "it's (a) thing".

On this card, someone guessed wrong, so 試作品です answers "What is it, then?": "It's a prototype." There's no word for "it". It's clear what he means, so Japanese leaves it out. That's what the [brackets] show.

Use it with strangers, clients and shops. With friends you'd say the casual version, 試作品だ: same meaning.

Casual

New Atashin'chi · Episode 1

ただの落書きだ

"[It's] just a scribble."

だ answers "What's that?" (ただの is "just a", 落書き is "scribble"). Use it with friends, family, or when thinking out loud.

Examples

A client asks what the sketch on your screen is.

これは表紙です。

"This is the cover."

Your friend asks what the sketch on your screen is, over coffee.

表紙だよ。

"It's the cover."

Someone at the post office asks where you're from.

オランダ人です。

"I'm Dutch."

You open the curtains in the morning and say it to yourself.

雨だ。

"It's raining."

With and without

です

雨です。

Polite. Strangers, clients, shops.

だ

雨だ。

Casual. Friends, or thinking out loud when you look outside.

Dropped

雨！

Super casual. Just the word. Totally normal with friends.

With よ

雨だよ。

"It's raining, FYI." Telling someone something they don't know.

The です family

PoliteCasual
isですだ
isn'tじゃないです
じゃありません		じゃない
wasでしただった
wasn'tじゃなかったです
じゃありませんでした		じゃなかった

In writing, じゃ becomes では.

Sentence mining

Polite

YouTube · video

これは生卵です。

"This is a raw egg."

生卵 ("raw egg") + です = "it's a raw egg". これは sets "this" as the topic: "this is...".

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 8

自家菜園です

"It's from my own vegetable garden."

自家菜園 ("home vegetable garden") + です, nothing else. The shortest polite answer there is.

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 1

ゾウガメです

"I'm a Galapagos tortoise."

ゾウガメ ("Galapagos tortoise") + です = "I'm a Galapagos tortoise". No word for "I": it's clear he means himself.

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 5

自信作ですよ

"It's my best work!"

自信作 ("my best work", something you're proud of) + です. よ: he's telling you something you didn't know.

Polite

YouTube · video

相撲は日本の国技です。

"Sumo is Japan's national sport."

相撲は ("as for sumo") + 日本の国技 ("Japan's national sport") + です. X は Y です = "X is Y".

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 2

お寿司屋さんみたいなメニューだね

"That's like a sushi restaurant menu, huh."

メニュー ("menu") + だ, the casual です. ね asks the other person to agree.

Casual

Pokémon: Indigo League · Episode 2

ろくに顔も分からないひどい写真だ。

"What a terrible photo, you can barely see the face."

ひどい写真 ("terrible photo") + だ = "it's a terrible photo". Everything before 写真 describes the photo.

Reference

A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

Entry "~wa ~da" · pp. 521–524

N5 Grammar

じゃない・ではありません

Politeじゃないです everyday, softer
じゃありません standard polite, a bit firmer
ではありません most formal: news, speeches, writing
Casualじゃない

Same meaning: "isn't". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

Pokémon: Indigo League · Episode 1

ボウヤじゃありません。

"[I'm] not a little boy."

じゃない says what something is NOT. It's the opposite of です / だ, and it goes in the same spot: right after a noun. Thing + じゃない = "it's not (a) thing".

On this card, Satoshi's been called ボウヤ ("little boy") and pushes back: ボウヤじゃありません, "I'm not a little boy." He's talking to an adult, so he says it politely.

Casual

Yu-Gi-Oh! · Season 0, Episode 1

はいおしまい、これは売り物じゃないんでな

"Okay, that's it. This isn't for sale."

Grandpa shuts down a customer: 売り物 ("something for sale") + じゃない = "not for sale". The んでな after it just means "so, you see".

Examples

A client points at a sketch and asks if it's the final cover.

いいえ、表紙じゃありません。

"No, it's not the cover."

Your friend asks the same thing over coffee.

表紙じゃないよ。

"It's not the cover."

Someone at the post office guesses you're German.

ドイツ人じゃないです。オランダ人です。

"I'm not German. I'm Dutch."

You look outside. The ground is wet, but nothing's falling.

雨じゃない。

"It's not raining."

The です family

PoliteCasual
isですだ
isn'tじゃないです
じゃありません		じゃない
wasでしただった
wasn'tじゃなかったです
じゃありませんでした		じゃなかった

In writing, じゃ becomes では.

Sentence mining

Polite

YouTube · video

このバスは貸切じゃないですよ。

"This bus isn't chartered, you know."

貸切 ("chartered, reserved") + じゃないです = "isn't chartered". よ: telling you something you didn't know.

Polite

YouTube · video

味噌じゃないけど、名古屋の手羽先も美味しいです。

"It's not miso, but Nagoya's chicken wings are tasty too."

A polite sentence (です at the end), but the じゃない in the middle stays plain. That's normal: only the end needs to be polite.

Polite

YouTube · video

もちろん今でも不満は尽きませんが、それでも今の自分は嫌いじゃありません

"Of course, I still have plenty of complaints, but even so, I don't dislike who I am now."

嫌い ends in い but it's a な-adjective, so it takes じゃありません like a noun. 嫌いじゃない is a modest way of saying "I kind of like it".

Polite

YouTube · video

実はこの作品を主導的に製作した金澤麻由子さんはコンピュータサイエンティストではありません

"Actually, Mayuko Kanazawa, who led the making of this work, isn't a computer scientist."

ではありません: the formal version of じゃありません, same meaning. You hear it in news, presentations and narration like this.

Casual

New Atashin'chi · Episode 1

それ動物虐待じゃねえの？

"Isn't that animal abuse?"

動物虐待 ("animal abuse") + じゃねえ, a rough, slangy じゃない (mostly guys, with friends). の？ makes it "isn't that...?".

Casual

Teasing Master Takagi-san · Season 1

いや、たいしたことじゃないよ。

"Nah, it's no big deal."

たいしたこと is "a big deal", じゃない makes it "not". The よ makes it reassuring.

Casual

YouTube · video

マヨラーじゃないけど、ケチャラ。

"I'm not a mayo person, but I'm a ketchup person."

マヨラー is slang for someone who puts mayo on everything. じゃないけど: "I'm not X, but...".

N5 Grammar

でした・だった

Politeでした
Casualだった

Same meaning: "was". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

YouTube · Let's learn Japanese in the city!!

これは昔、山形県の県庁でした。

"This used to be the Yamagata prefectural office."

でした is the past of です: it says what something was. It goes in the same spot, right after a noun. Thing + でした = "it was (a) thing".

On this card, the guide stands in front of an old building and tells you what it used to be. 昔 ("long ago") sets the time, でした closes it in the past.

Casual

New Atashin'chi · Episode 1

ほーら楽勝…だった。

"See? Piece of cake... [it] was."

Mom squeezes onto a packed train: 楽勝 ("a breeze") + だった = "it was a breeze". Her squashed face says otherwise.

Examples

A coworker asks what you did before design.

前は先生でした。

"I used to be a teacher."

Your friend asks the same thing over drinks.

前は先生だったよ。

"I used to be a teacher."

The hotel staff asks about the weather on your trip.

ずっと雨でした。

"It rained the whole time."

雨 ("rain") + でした = "it was rain". ずっと: "the whole time".

You check the old receipt. The coffee was free.

あ、タダだった。

"Oh, it was free."

With and without

だ

雨だ。

"It's raining." Now.

だった

雨だった。

"It was raining." Before. Casual.

です

雨です。

"It's raining." Now. Polite.

でした

雨でした。

"It was raining." Before. Polite. Never だったです: the past is already in でした.

The です family

PoliteCasual
isですだ
isn'tじゃないです
じゃありません		じゃない
wasでしただった
wasn'tじゃなかったです
じゃありませんでした		じゃなかった

In writing, じゃ becomes では.

Sentence mining

Polite

YouTube · video

じゃあ、おまけでした。

"Okay, that was the bonus."

おまけ ("bonus, extra") + でした = "that was the bonus". Once something is over, it becomes でした.

Polite

YouTube · video

あの、なんかちょっとあの、現代的な美術館でしたね。

"Um, it was kind of a modern art museum, huh."

現代的な美術館 ("modern art museum") + でした = "it was a modern art museum". ね: looking back on it together.

Polite

1 Litre of Tears · Episode 11

亜也さんはすごい人でした。

"Aya was an amazing person."

すごい人 ("amazing person") + でした = "was an amazing person".

Casual

YouTube · video

ああ、骸骨だった。

"Ah, it was a skeleton."

骸骨 ("skeleton") + だった = "it was a skeleton". Talking to himself, so casual.

Casual

Girls Band Cry · Episode 4

ずっと夢だった。

"It was always my dream."

夢 ("dream") + だった = "was my dream". ずっと ("all along") means it was true for a long time.

Casual

From Up on Poppy Hill

私達は親友だった。

"We were best friends."

親友 ("best friend") + だった = "were best friends".

Casual

Border · Episode 6

何より 優しい人だった。

"Above all, he was kind."

優しい人 ("kind person") + だった = "was a kind person". 何より: "above all".

N5 Grammar

じゃなかった・ではありませんでした

Politeじゃなかったです everyday, softer
じゃありませんでした standard polite, a bit firmer
ではありませんでした most formal: news, speeches, writing
Casualじゃなかった everyday
ではなかった stiffer: writing, serious talk

Same meaning: "wasn't". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

Frieren · Episode 12

今回の勇者も 本物ではありませんでしたか。

"So this hero wasn't the real one either?"

ではありませんでした says what something was not. It goes right after a noun, in the same spot as です. Noun + ではありませんでした = "it wasn't (a) noun".

On this card, someone asks whether a hero was genuine: 本物 ("the real deal") + ではありませんでした = "wasn't the real deal". も means "this one too, like the ones before", and か turns it into a question.

Casual

Weakest Beast · Episode 5

愛じゃなかった。

"That wasn't love."

On this card, she looks back and says what it really wasn't: 愛 ("love") + じゃなかった = "it wasn't love".

Examples

You open the box from the online shop. Wrong item.

え、これじゃなかった。

"Huh, it wasn't this one."

You tell the shop staff the same thing on the phone.

注文したのはこれじゃありませんでした。

"What I ordered wasn't this."

A coworker asks if yesterday was your day off.

いや、休みじゃなかったです。

"No, it wasn't my day off."

You thought you saw a friend at the station. You didn't.

あれ、ケンじゃなかった。

"Oh, that wasn't Ken."

With and without

じゃない

休みじゃない。

"It's not a day off."

じゃなかった

休みじゃなかった。

"It wasn't a day off." ない → なかった.

The です family

PoliteCasual
isですだ
isn'tじゃないです
じゃありません		じゃない
wasでしただった
wasn'tじゃなかったです
じゃありませんでした		じゃなかった

In writing, じゃ becomes では.

Sentence mining

Polite

Frieren · Episode 6

いい対応ではありませんでしたね。

"That wasn't a very warm welcome."

いい対応 ("a good welcome") + ではありませんでした = "wasn't a good welcome". ね at the end: "was it?", expecting you to agree.

Polite

Fermat Kitchen · Episode 2

このパスタは アルデンテでは ありませんでしたよね。

"This pasta wasn't al dente, was it?"

アルデンテ ("al dente", firm to the bite) + ではありませんでした = "wasn't al dente". よね: "right?", checking you noticed it too.

Polite

Little Witch Academia · Episode 19

わたくしも 嫌いではありませんでした。

"I didn't dislike it either."

嫌い ("dislike") + ではありませんでした = "didn't dislike it". 嫌い is a な-adjective, but there's no な before では. も: "either".

Polite

Mob Psycho 100 · Episode 1

大した霊じゃなかったですよ。

"It wasn't much of a ghost."

大した霊 ("much of a ghost") + じゃなかったです = "wasn't much of a ghost". よ: telling the other person something they don't know yet.

Casual

My Neighbor Totoro

夢じゃなかった！ 夢だけど！

"It wasn't a dream! Even though it was a dream!"

In the night they saw Totoro grow a giant tree. In the morning, real sprouts are there: it wasn't a dream! But it also kind of was one (夢だけど).

Casual

Demon Slayer - Kimetsu no Yaiba · Episode 21

俺たちの絆は 本物じゃなかった。

"Our bond wasn't real."

俺たちの絆は ("our bond") is the topic. 本物 ("the real thing") + じゃなかった = "wasn't real".

Casual

From Up on Poppy Hill

私の苦労は 無駄ではなかった！

"My hard work wasn't for nothing!"

無駄 ("a waste") + ではなかった = "wasn't a waste". ではなかった sounds weightier than じゃなかった, which suits a big emotional moment.

Casual

Legal High · Episode 7

認知症ではなかったと？

"You're saying there was no dementia?"

認知症 ("dementia") + ではなかった = "wasn't dementia". と？ at the end repeats someone's claim back: "you're saying...?"

N5 Grammar

は

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 5

それは剣道

"That [is] kendo."

は marks the topic: what the sentence is about. It goes right after a noun, and then you say something about it: それ + は + 剣道 = "as for that: kendo".

On this card, it answers "What's that?". それは sets the topic ("that"), 剣道 is what gets said about it. There's no だ at the end: in casual speech it often gets dropped, which is what the [brackets] show.

Written は, said "wa". Once everyone knows the topic, it gets dropped too: just 剣道 would also work as an answer.

Examples

Meeting a new client. You introduce yourself.

私はセブです。

"As for me, I'm Seb."

A friend asks if you're free this week.

今日は忙しい。明日は大丈夫。

"Today, I'm busy. Tomorrow, I'm fine."

At dinner, someone offers you meat and fish.

魚は食べます。

"Fish, I do eat." (meat, maybe not)

With and without

Without

魚、食べる。

"I eat fish." Plain and casual.

With は

魚は食べる。

"Fish, I eat." Hints there's something else you don't.

Sentence mining

Polite

YouTube · video

私は車酔いもしやすいです。

"I also get carsick easily."

As for me... Like 私はセブです: は sets the topic (me), then comes the comment.

Polite

YouTube · video

今日は二度寝しました。

"Today I fell back asleep after waking up."

Time words like 今日 often get は: as for today... 二度寝 is going back to sleep.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 12

僕はミルフィーユ

"I'll have the mille-feuille."

Ordering: as for me, mille-feuille. Literally "I am mille-feuille", but は just means "as for me".

Casual

YouTube · video

水道代は0円

"Water bill: zero yen."

As for the water bill... zero. A short caption, no です needed.

Polite

YouTube · video

試合は互角の勝負でした。

"The match was a close fight."

試合 ("the match") + は: as for the match... 互角の勝負 ("an even fight") + でした.

Casual

New Atashin'chi · Episode 1

こういう時は強気でいかなきゃね。

"At times like this, you've got to be bold."

は can set a situation as the topic too, not just a person or thing: as for times like this...

Polite

YouTube · video

醤油の量はお好みです。

"How much soy sauce is up to you."

As for the amount of soy sauce... は sets the topic, then comes the comment: your choice.

Polite

YouTube · video

お釣りはちょっと面倒くさいです。

"Getting change is a bit of a hassle."

お釣り ("change") + は: as for change... ちょっと面倒くさい ("a bit of a hassle").

Reference

A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

Entry "wa¹" (は) · pp. 516–519

N5 Grammar

か

Polite～ですか after nouns and adjectives
～ますか after verbs
Casual～か

Both turn a sentence into a question. Casual speech often drops か and just raises the voice.

Polite

YouTube · video

レジ袋いりますか？

"Do you need a bag?" [the cashier, at the till]

か at the end turns a sentence into a question. It's a spoken question mark.

It goes right after the polite ending: いります → いりますか, です → ですか. On this card, the cashier asks a yes/no question: bag or no bag?

In casual speech you usually drop か and just raise your voice: いる？

Casual

New Atashin'chi · Episode 1

しとめたか？

"Did I get it?"

Casual か goes straight after a plain verb or a noun, with no です and no だ: しとめたか, 罠か (never 罠だか). It sounds blunt, so you mostly hear it from guys, or from someone asking themself.

Examples

You're on a platform, not sure about the train. You ask the person next to you.

この電車は渋谷に行きますか？

"Does this train go to Shibuya?"

Polite

At a party, someone you just met mentions their exams.

学生ですか？

"Are you a student?"

Polite

Your phone died and you ask a shop clerk.

今何時ですか？

"What time is it?"

Polite, with a question word

Texting a friend about tomorrow's barbecue.

明日来る？

"You coming tomorrow?"

Casual, no か

With and without

Without

レジ袋いります。

"I need a bag." You're telling the cashier.

With か

レジ袋いりますか？

"Do you need a bag?" The cashier is asking you.

Casual, no か

袋いる？

"Need a bag?" Normal, friendly. Just a rising voice.

Casual with か

袋いるか？

"Need a bag or not?" Blunt, like a gruff dad.

Sentence mining

Polite

YouTube · video

力加減は大丈夫ですか？

"Is the pressure okay?"

At the hair salon, checking with the customer. Adjective + ですか: yes or no, is it okay?

Polite

YouTube · video

失礼ですが、火星人ですか？

"Excuse me, but are you a Martian?"

A weird question, but a polite one. 失礼ですが ("excuse me, but") softens it before the ですか.

Polite

YouTube · video

この作業部屋は自宅ですか？

"Is this workroom in your home?"

Interviewer asking a stranger, so ですか. Yes or no: home, or an office?

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 4

なんか　小さくて字　読みづらくないですか？

"Isn't the text kind of small and hard to read?"

ですか on a negative = "isn't it?", asking them to agree.

Polite

Weakest Beast · Episode 3

出張ですか？

"A business trip?"

出張 ("business trip") + ですか = "a business trip?". です + か turns any statement into a question.

Polite

Spirited Away

お呼びですか。

"Did you call for me?"

お呼び ("calling for someone", polite) + ですか = "did you call me?". Even with a falling voice, か makes it a question.

Casual

PiroPito · First Playthrough of Minecraft #04

原木から、作れるってことか

"So you can make it from logs, huh."

Plain form + か, said to himself. He's not asking anyone, he's figuring it out out loud.

Reference

A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

Entry "ka²" (question marker) · pp. 166–168

N5 Grammar

これ・それ・あれ

YouTube · video

これは急須です

"This is a teapot."

これ, それ and あれ mean "this thing" or "that thing". Which one you pick depends on where the thing is: これ is near me, それ is near you, あれ is far from both of us.

On this card, she's holding the teapot in her hand, so it's これ. If you were holding it, she'd say それは急須です.

They work like normal nouns, so particles go right after: これは, それが, あれを.

Examples

At the konbini, you hold up an onigiri you don't recognise.

これは何ですか？

"What's this?"

It's in your hand: これ.

A friend shows you their new camera.

それ、いくらだった？

"How much was that?"

It's in their hand: それ.

On the beach in Chigasaki, you spot an island far out at sea.

あれは江の島？

"Is that Enoshima?"

Far from both of you: あれ.

A friend says they're moving to Kyoto.

それはいいね。

"That's great."

それ also points at something the other person just said.

With and without

With これ

これは何ですか？

Points at the thing. Clear even if there are several things around.

Without

何ですか？

When you're already holding it up, Japanese often just leaves これ out.

Sentence mining

Polite

YouTube · video

それは長ねぎですよ。

"That's a leek."

The leek is in the alien's hand, not hers, so それ.

Polite

YouTube · video

これ、ほんの気持ちです。

"This is just a small token of thanks."

Handing over a gift: it's still in your hands, so これ. The は is dropped here.

Polite

YouTube · video

これはニット帽です。

"This is a knit hat."

これは + ニット帽 ("knit hat") + です = "this is a knit hat". It's in her hands, so これ.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 1

それはひまわり。

"That's a sunflower."

Casual: no です, the sentence just stops after the noun.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 4

それは　ダンク

"That's a dunk."

Correcting what the other person just did or said. それ for their thing.

Casual

New Atashin'chi · Episode 1

これは究極の兵器かもねえ。

"This might be the ultimate weapon."

It's in the speaker's hands, so これ. 究極の兵器 ("the ultimate weapon") + かもねえ ("might be").

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 2

それは卓袱台。

"That's a low dining table."

The table is next to the other person, so それ.

N5 Grammar

この・その・あの

YouTube · video

この自転車は借りた自転車です。

"This bike is a rented bike."

この, その and あの mean "this ___" or "that ___", and a noun always comes right after: この自転車, その本, あの人. Which one depends on where the thing is: この is near me, その is near you, あの is far from both of us.

On this card, he's sitting on the bike, so it's この自転車. It answers "which bike?": this one, the one I'm on.

They never stand alone. Without a noun you use これ, それ, あれ instead: これは借りた自転車です.

Examples

At a bakery, you point at a bread in the case right in front of you.

このパンをください。

"This bread, please."

Near you: この.

A friend is wearing a jacket you like.

そのジャケット、どこで買ったの？

"Where did you buy that jacket?"

It's on them: その.

You and a friend see a tall tower in the distance.

あのビルは何？

"What's that building?"

Far from both of you: あの.

A friend mentions a ramen place they went to last week.

その店、どこ？

"Where's that place?"

その also points at something the other person just talked about.

With and without

Without a noun

これは高いです。

"This is expensive." これ is the thing itself.

With この

この時計は高いです。

"This watch is expensive." この needs a noun after it.

Without a noun

あれは何？

"What's that?" You don't say what kind of thing.

With あの

あの鳥は何？

N5 Grammar

ここ・そこ・あそこ

YouTube · video

え、ここは出汁のお店です。

"So, this place is a dashi shop."

ここ, そこ and あそこ mean "here" and "there". They point at a place, not a thing. Same split as これ・それ・あれ: ここ is where I am, そこ is near you, あそこ is far from both of us.

On this card, she's standing at the shop, so it's ここ. It answers "Where are we?": ここは sets the topic (this place), 出汁のお店です says what it is.

They work like normal nouns, so particles go right after: ここは, そこに, あそこで.

Examples

A friend visits your new flat. You open the door to one room.

ここは私の部屋です。

"This is my room."

You're standing in it: ここ.

At a café, there's an empty chair next to someone.

そこ、座ってもいいですか？

"May I sit there?"

The seat is next to them: そこ.

In a taxi, you see your hotel at the end of the street.

あそこで止めてください。

"Please stop over there."

Far from you and the driver: あそこ.

With and without

With これ

これは駅です。

"This is a station." Pointing at a thing, like a station on a map.

With ここ

ここは駅です。

"This place is a station." You're standing in it.

N5 Grammar

こちら・そちら・あちら

Politeこちら・そちら・あちら
Casualこっち・そっち・あっち

Same meaning: "this way, that way". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

"This is a work that blends painting and manga."

こちら, そちら and あちら point at a side or a direction: "this way", "that way". Same split as ここ・そこ・あそこ: こちら is near me, そちら is near you, あちら is far from both of us.

They're also the polite "here" and "this one". Staff, guides and presenters say こちら instead of ここ or これ. On this card, she's showing a piece to visitors, so こちらは answers "What's this one?"

They work like nouns: こちらは, こちらに, こちらの + noun.

Far from both of you: あっち (casual あちら).

N5 Grammar

がある

Politeあります
Casualある

Same meaning: "there is". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

YouTube · video

背もたれがあります。

"[The chair] has a backrest."

がある says something exists: "there is", or "it has / I have". The thing goes first, then が, then ある. It's for things, places and events, not for people or animals (those use いる).

On this card, she's showing a chair and answers "What does it have?": a backrest. 背もたれ + が + あります.

"There isn't" is ありません / ない.

Casual

YouTube · Road to Vostok #1

あ、なんかあそこにお店屋さんみたいなとこある

"Oh, there's some kind of shop-looking place over there."

In casual talk the が often drops out, like here: とこ ある instead of とこがある.

Examples

A tourist asks if there's a convenience store nearby.

駅の前にコンビニがありますよ。

"There's a convenience store in front of the station."

Where first (駅の前に), then what (コンビニ), then があります.

Polite

A coworker asks if you can go for drinks tomorrow.

明日はテストがあります。

"I have a test tomorrow."

Events work too: a test, a meeting, plans.

Polite

Your friend opens your fridge.

ビールある？

"Is there any beer?"

Casual question: no が, no か, just a rising voice.

Casual

A friend wants to watch one more episode.

もう時間がない。

"There's no time left."

The "not" of ある is ない (never あらない).

Casual

Without

"It's a backrest." You're naming the thing.

With がある

"It has a backrest." You're saying it's there.

Without

時間です。

"It's time." Time to go, time to start.

With がある

"I have time." The time exists, you're free.

N5 Grammar

がいる

Politeいます
Casualいる

Same meaning: "there is" (people, animals). Only the politeness changes.

Polite

YouTube · video

なんか、このレストランにはたくさん芸術家がいます！

"Like, there are lots of artists in this restaurant!"

がいる says someone is there: "there is", or "I have" for people. The person or animal goes first, then が, then いる. Things use ある instead.

On this card, she looks around the restaurant and answers "Who's here?": lots of artists. 芸術家 + が + います.

"There isn't" is いません / いない.

Examples

You call a shop and ask if the manager is in.

今、店長がいますか？

"Is the manager there right now?"

Add か and it's a question: "is someone there?".

Polite

A coworker asks about your family.

姉がいます。

"I have an older sister."

"I have" a person is also いる: brothers, kids, friends.

Polite

あ、猫がいる。

Animals are いる too, even tiny ones like spiders.

Casual

The "not" of いる is いない. 誰もいない: "nobody is there".

Sounds like a friend is an object you own.

With がいる

"I have a friend." People take いる.

N5 Grammar

～たち

YouTube · video

子どもたちも農作業を楽しんでいます。

"The children are also enjoying the farm work."

たち turns one person into a group of people: 子ども (a child) becomes 子どもたち (children). It goes right after the word.

On this card, it answers "just one, or several?": here it's several kids. Japanese doesn't mark plurals otherwise, so たち is how you say "we", "they", "the kids".

It's used for people (and sometimes animals), not for things. Same in polite and casual speech.

Examples

You and your friend are talking about the weekend.

私たちは土曜日に会います。

"We're meeting on Saturday."

私 (I) + たち = 私たち (we). The same works for 僕たち and 俺たち.

A student asks where the teachers are.

先生たちは会議室にいます。

"The teachers are in the meeting room."

Talking about a group of girls over there.

あの子たちは双子です。

"Those kids are twins."

The group word (あの子) can be a person, and たち makes it "those kids".

With and without

Without

私は公園に行きます。

I'm going to the park. Just me.

With たち

私たちは公園に行きます。

We're going to the park. Me and others.

N5 Grammar

何 (なに・なん)

YouTube · video

日本に帰ってまず何をしますか?

"What's the first thing you'll do when you get back to Japan?"

何 means "what". It asks for a thing, and it sits right where that thing would go in the answer. Here it's the thing you do, so it takes を like any object.

On this card, the answer would be: まずラーメンを食べます. Same shape, 何 swapped for ラーメン.

It's read なに here. Before です, だ, の and counters it turns into なん: 何ですか？ (なんですか). Casual just drops ます: 何する？

Examples

A friend hands you a snack you've never seen.

これ、何？

"What's this?"

Casual: これ ("this") + 何 with a rising voice. Read なに when it stands alone.

Casual

At a restaurant, you point at the menu.

これは何ですか？

"What is this?"

Before です it's なん: なんですか.

Polite

Friday night, texting a friend.

週末、何する？

"What are you doing this weekend?"

何 + する, no particle needed in casual speech.

Casual

You left your watch at home.

すみません、今何時ですか？

"Excuse me, what time is it now?"

何 + a counter is always なん: 何時 (なんじ), 何人 (なんにん).

Polite

With and without

With a thing

週末、映画を見ます。

"I'll watch a movie this weekend." You already know what.

With 何

週末、何を見ますか？

"What will you watch this weekend?" Swap the thing for 何, add か, and it's a question.

N5 Grammar

誰 (だれ)・どなた

Politeどなた
Casual誰 (だれ)

Same meaning: "who". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 8

このステキなアレンジメントはどなたが？

"Who [made] this lovely arrangement?"

誰 (だれ) means "who". どなた is the polite version, for customers, strangers and people above you.

It sits where the person would go in the answer, and keeps the same particle: 店長が作りました → どなたが？ On this card, the verb is simply dropped.

Casual: このアレンジメント、誰が作ったの？

Examples

A friend points at a photo on your phone.

この人、誰？

"Who's this?"

Between friends, just 誰. No です, no か.

Casual

Someone knocks on your door.

どなたですか？

"Who is it?"

どなた (the polite 誰) + です + か. どなた works like a noun, so です goes right after it.

Polite

The last piece of cake is gone.

誰が食べたの？

"Who ate it?"

Asking who DID something: 誰が. Not 誰は.

Casual

An umbrella is left in the office.

"Whose umbrella is this?"

誰の = "whose", same の as 私の.

Polite

With a person

"Tanaka came." You already know who.

With 誰

"Who came?" Swap the person for 誰, keep が, add か.

N5 Grammar

どこ

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 3

ママ！　人魚さん　どこ？

"Mom! Where's the mermaid?"

どこ means "where". It asks for a place, and it sits right where the place would go in the answer.

On this card, the kid wants to know where the mermaid is, so it's 人魚さん + どこ. The answer just swaps どこ for a place: 人魚さんはあそこ ("over there").

Casual is just どこ？ like here. Polite adds です and か: 人魚さんはどこですか？

Examples

At a station, you ask a staff member.

トイレはどこですか？

"Where's the toilet?"

Answer: トイレはあそこです. Same shape, どこ swapped for あそこ.

Polite

You're at the café, your friend is late. You text them.

今どこ？

"Where are you now?"

Between friends, just どこ. No です, no か.

Casual

A friend has a nice new jacket.

どこで買ったの？

"Where did you buy it?"

どこ works like a normal noun, so particles go right after. で = where something happens.

Casual

Meeting someone new.

"Where do you live?"

に = where someone or something is.

Polite

With あそこ

"The station is over there." You already know the place.

With どこ

駅はどこですか？

"Where is the station?" Swap the place for どこ, add か, and it's a question.

"Hmm, where should I build my house? It's so peaceful here."

どこに + a verb = where to do it. に marks the spot the house will go.

Casual

I'm Taking the Day Off · Episode 7

どこにやった？

"Where did you put it?"

どこ + に ("to") + やった ("put, sent") = "where did you put it?".

Casual

Overprotected Kahoko · Episode 5

どこ行くんだ？

"Where's she going?"

どこ + 行く ("go"): casual speech drops the へ or に. んだ asks for an explanation.

Casual

Overprotected Kahoko · Episode 7

どこがいい？

"Where would you like to go?"

どこ + が + いい ("good") = "where is good?", asking someone's choice of place.

Casual

From Up on Poppy Hill

お家はどこ？

"Where's your house?"

お家 ("house", polite) + は + どこ = "where's your house?". X は どこ asks where X is.

Casual

The Secret World of Arrietty

ここはどこなの？

"Where is this place?"

ここ ("here") + は + どこ = "where is this place?". なの makes it a soft, puzzled question.

Polite

My Neighbor Totoro

これ、どこへ運びます？

"Where should I take this?"

どこ + へ ("to") + 運びます ("carry") = "where should I carry this?".

N5 Grammar

いつ

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 4

シロクマくん　免許はいつ取ったの？

"Shirokuma, when did you get your license?"

いつ means "when". It asks for a time, and it sits where the time would go in the answer: 去年取った ("I got it last year").

No particle after it: いつ取った, not いつに. A real time does take に (3時に), but いつ never does.

On this card, it's casual (取ったの？). Polite: 免許はいつ取りましたか？

Polite

YouTube · 73 Easy Japanese Questions

最近いつ落ち込みましたか?最近はね、全然落ち込んでいませんね。

"When did you last feel down? Lately? I haven't been down at all."

Polite version: same spot for いつ, still no に, and the verb gets ます.

Examples

A friend says they're going to Japan.

いつ行くの？

"When are you going?"

Casual

Chatting with a coworker.

誕生日はいつですか？

"When is your birthday?"

いつ works like a noun, so です goes right after it.

Polite

Your classmate is studying hard.

試験はいつ？

"When's the exam?"

Between friends, just いつ. No です, no か.

Casual

A shop is closed. You ask someone outside.

いつ開きますか？

"When does it open?"

Polite

With and without

With a time

明日行きます。

"I'll go tomorrow." You already know when.

With いつ

いつ行きますか？

"When will you go?" Swap the time for いつ, add か. No に.

Polite

Source unknown No source

いつ初めて、母国語以外の言葉を使って話しましたか？

"When did you first speak in a language other than your native one?"

いつ right at the start, straight into the verb. No に.

Polite

Border · Episode 7

最後に会ったのは いつですか？

"When did you last see him?"

〜のは いつですか: when was it that ...?

Polite

The Journalist · Episode 6

いつからですか？

"Since when?"

いつ + から ("from") + ですか = "since when?".

Casual

1 Litre of Tears · Episode 4

いつ帰ってくるの？

"When is she coming home?"

いつ goes right before the verb, no particle.

Casual

Overprotected Kahoko · Episode 5

へえ～ じゃあ いつ帰んのよ？

"Then when are you going home?"

いつ + 帰んの (casual 帰るの, "go home") = "when are you going home?". No particle after いつ.

Casual

Quartet · Episode 3

あいつ いつ来んのかな？

"I wonder when she's coming."

いつ + 来んの (casual 来るの, "come") + かな ("I wonder") = "I wonder when she's coming".

Polite

Weakest Beast · Episode 2

この前の人 いつ来るんすか？

"When's that guy from before coming?"

来るんすか: sloppy polite 来るんですか.

N5 Grammar

どれ・どの

YouTube · video

どれにしようかな

"Which one should I go with?"

どれ means "which one", picking from three or more things. It stands on its own, like これ・それ・あれ.

どの asks the same, but needs a noun right after it: どのケーキ ("which cake"). Same pair as これ and この.

On this card, にする = "go with, decide on", かな = "I wonder". Polite: どれにしますか？

Examples

At a bakery with a full display.

どれがいい？

"Which one do you want?"

Casual

Asking the staff.

どれがおすすめですか？

"Which one do you recommend?"

Polite

At a big station, asking for help.

どの電車に乗りますか？

"Which train do I take?"

どの + noun (電車). どの never stands alone.

Polite

A friend shows you a class photo.

どの人？

"Which person?"

Casual

With and without

With これ

これがいいです。

"This one is good." You've already picked.

With どれ

どれがいいですか？

"Which one is good?" Swap これ for どれ. Before a noun it's この → どの.

Sentence mining

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 3

ねえねえ　どの寝顔が　いちばん好き？

"Hey hey, which sleeping face do you like best?"

どの + noun (寝顔, "sleeping face"), picking from a bunch of photos.

Casual

1 Litre of Tears · Episode 6

"Which one should I get?"

どれにしよう: which one should I pick?

Casual

Weakest Beast · Episode 4

ゴーヤー麺、どれがいい？

"Bitter melon noodles... which one do you want?"

どれがいい: which one is good for you?

Polite

I'm Taking the Day Off · Episode 6

どの辺がですか？

"Which part?"

どの + 辺 ("part, area") + がですか = "which part?". どの always needs a noun after it.

Casual

I am Mita, Your Housekeeper · Episode 9

どれもおいしいな。

"They're all delicious."

どれ + も = "every one of them". おいしい ("delicious") + な: said to himself.

Casual

Weakest Beast · Episode 9

誰が どれを？

"Who gets which?"

誰が ("who") + どれを ("which one"): "who gets which?", with the verb left out.

Casual

どれが一番好き？

"Which do you like best?"

どれ + が + 一番好き ("like best") = "which do you like best?", out of three or more.

N5 Grammar

どちら・どっち

Politeどちら
Casualどっち

Same meaning: "which one (of two)". Only the politeness changes.

YouTube · video

みなさんは、海と山だったら、どっち派ですか？

"Everyone, sea or mountains: which are you more into?"

どっち means "which one", picking between two things. On this card: the sea or the mountains (派 = "camp, type").

どちら is the polite version, どっち the casual one. People mix them, like here: casual どっち, polite です.

どちら is also the polite way to ask "where" or "which way": 駅はどちらですか？

Examples

Holding up two shirts for a friend.

どっちがいい？

"Which one is better?"

Casual

A waiter at a café.

コーヒーと紅茶、どちらがいいですか？

"Coffee or tea, which would you like?"

Polite

Lost, asking a stranger.

駅はどちらですか？

"Which way is the station?"

A politer どこ.

Polite

Small talk with a friend.

犬と猫、どっちが好き？

"Dogs or cats, which do you like?"

Casual

With and without

With どれ (3 or more)

どれがいい？

"Which one do you want?" From a whole row of things.

With どっち (two)

赤と青、どっちがいい？

"Red or blue, which do you want?" Only two to choose from.

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 9

で　お届けはどちらまで

"And where shall we deliver it to?"

どちら as a polite どこ, the way shop staff talk. まで = "to, as far as".

Polite

Border · Episode 2

どちら様ですか？

"Who is it?"

どちら様: the polite "who?", at the door or on the phone.

Polite

ご遺骨はどちらに？

"Where are his ashes?"

ご遺骨 ("his ashes", polite) + は + どちら + に: "where are they?". どちら is the polite どこ.

Polite

Legal High · Episode 11

黛先生は今 どちらの事務所で？

"Which firm are you at now, Mayuzumi-sensei?"

どちら + の + 事務所 ("office, firm") = "which firm?". どちらの is the polite どの.

Polite

Death Note · Episode 10

ではどちらにするか決めてください。

"Then please decide which it will be."

どちら + に + する ("decide on") = "decide which one". か makes it "whether this or that".

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 9

で、お届けはどちらまで？

"So, where should we deliver it?"

お届け ("delivery") + は + どちらまで ("as far as where?"): shop staff asking for the address.

Casual

I am Mita, Your Housekeeper · Episode 11

どっちか選びなさい。

"Pick one of the two."

どっち (casual どちら) + か = "one of the two". 選びなさい = "choose!", an order.

N5 Grammar

どう・いかが

Politeどうですか everyday polite
いかがですか extra polite, for offers
Casualどう

Same meaning: "how, how about". Only the politeness changes.

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 5

どうしたの？何か考え事？

"What's wrong? Thinking about something?"

どう means "how" or "how about". It asks what something is like or how it went, not for a thing or a place.

On this card, どうした = "how did it go, what happened (to you)". It's the go-to line when someone looks off.

Polite: どうしましたか？ いかが is an extra polite どう, mostly for offers: コーヒーはいかがですか？

Examples

Your friend tries the ramen you recommended.

味はどう？

"How does it taste?"

Casual

A teacher asks a new student.

日本の生活はどうですか？

"How's life in Japan?"

Polite

A café staff member, holding a jug.

お水はいかがですか？

"Would you like some water?"

いかが = very polite どう. Staff use it to offer things.

Polite

Planning to meet up.

明日はどう？

"How about tomorrow?"

どう also suggests something: "how about ___?"

Casual

With and without

With 何

何を見た？

"What did you watch?" Asks for a thing.

With どう

映画はどうだった？

"How was the movie?" Asks what it was like.

Polite

YouTube · video

どうやってその大変な時悲しい時を乗り越えましたか

"How did you get through those hard, sad times?"

どうやって = "how, in what way". It asks for the method.

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 22

駅前でポケットティッシュと一緒に配るのはどうでしょう？

"How about handing them out with pocket tissues in front of the station?"

どうでしょう = a soft, polite "how about ___?" for suggesting an idea.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 3

どうしたの？　クイズ出す？

"What's up? Want to give us a quiz?"

どうしたの again, here just a friendly "what's up?"

Casual

Overprotected Kahoko · Episode 7

どういう意味？

"What do you mean?"

どう + いう ("say") + 意味 ("meaning") = "what do you mean?". どういう + noun = "what kind of".

Casual

Border · Episode 1

どうだ？

"Well? How is it?"

どう + だ: a rough, casual "how is it?", waiting for a reaction.

Casual

The Journalist · Episode 2

"What's wrong?"

どう + した ("did") = "what happened?", the usual way to ask "what's wrong?".

Casual

"So, what'll it be?"

どう + する ("do") = "what will you do?". さぁ: "so, well then".

N5 Grammar

どんな

Casual

YouTube · Japanese Listening Practice #101

江戸弁ってどんな感じ？

"What's Edo dialect like?"

どんな means "what kind of". It always comes right before a noun: どんな + 感じ ("feel").

So it asks you to describe something. The answer is a describing word + the noun: 優しい感じ ("a gentle feel").

On this card, って is casual は. Polite: 江戸弁はどんな感じですか？

Polite

YouTube · video

どんな髪型が似合うと思いますか？

"What kind of hairstyle do you think suits me?"

Same どんな + noun (髪型, "hairstyle"), polite with ます.

Examples

Your friend has a new boyfriend.

どんな人？

"What's he like?"

Answer: 優しい人 ("a kind person").

Casual

Getting to know someone.

どんな音楽が好きですか？

"What kind of music do you like?"

Polite

A friend just moved.

どんな部屋？

"What's the room like?"

Casual

Asking someone from Kyoto.

京都はどんなところですか？

"What kind of place is Kyoto?"

Polite

With and without

With 何

好きな音楽は何ですか？

"What music do you like?" Wants a name: ジャズ.

With どんな

どんな音楽が好きですか？

"What kind of music do you like?" Wants a description: 静かな音楽.

どんな + 小屋 ("hut"). のでしょうか = a soft "I wonder".

どんな + コンビニ. 1番 = "the most".

どんな + 服 ("clothes") = "what kind of clothes?". だよ makes it a bit pushy.

"Hm... what's he like?"

どんな + 人 ("person") = "what kind of person?", the usual way to ask "what's he like?".

どんな + ふうに ("in a way") = "in what way?", "like how?".

"Like what?"

どんな + こと ("thing") = "what kind of thing?", "like what?".

N5 Grammar

どうして・なぜ

Politeどうしてですか everyday polite
なぜですか stiff, formal, written
Casualどうして everyday
なんで most casual, spoken

Same meaning: "why". Only the politeness changes.

Casual

Pokémon The Series: Indigo League · Episode 2

どうしてネコがネズミに負けるのよ！

"Why would a cat lose to a mouse?!"

どうして means "why". It goes at or near the start and asks for a reason.

The answer usually ends in から ("because") or んです: ネズミが強いから ("because the mouse is strong").

On this card, のよ is just Meowth being annoyed.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 2

なんでまた僕

"Why me again?"

なんで is the everyday spoken "why". The most casual of the three, used with friends all the time.

Examples

Your friend left the party early.

どうして帰ったの？

"Why did you go home?"

Casual

A teacher asks a new student.

どうして日本語を勉強していますか？

"Why are you studying Japanese?"

Polite

Your friend shows up an hour late.

なんで遅れたの？

"Why were you late?"

なんで: the most natural one between friends.

Casual

In a work meeting.

なぜですか？

"Why is that?"

なぜ sounds stiff in speech. You'll mostly see it in news and titles.

Polite

With and without

Just the fact

昨日、休みました。

"I took yesterday off."

With どうして

どうして休みましたか？

"Why did you take the day off?" Answer: 熱があったから ("because I had a fever").

"Mr. Kuwano, why did you become an architect?"

なられた is an extra respectful なった ("became"). んですか asks for the story behind it, see ～んです.

Polite

どうしてですか？

"Why is that?"

どうして + ですか = "why is that?". Polite, but softer than なぜですか.

Casual

"Why do you want to move out?"

どうして at the start, の at the end to ask for the reason.

Casual

"How do you know?"

どうして + 分かる ("know, understand") = "how come you know?". の at the end asks for the reason.

どうして？

"Why?"

Just どうして with a rising voice: "why?".

Casual

"Wh-why..."

どうして on its own, trailing off: a shocked "why...".

"Why?"

どうして said flat, almost to herself: "why?".

N5 Grammar

いくら

Examples

At a market stall, pointing at a bag.

このかばんはいくらですか？

"How much is this bag?"

いくら sits where the price would go: このかばんは3000円です.

Polite

Your friend shows you their new shoes.

それ、いくらだった？

"How much were they?"

Past price: いくらだった (casual), いくらでしたか (polite).

Casual

Getting into a taxi.

駅までいくらぐらいですか？

"About how much is it to the station?"

ぐらい after it makes it "about how much".

Polite

The waiter brings the bill. You ask your friend.

いくら？

"How much?"

Between friends, just いくら. No です, no か.

Casual

A shop clerk tells you the total.

おいくらですか？

"How much is it?"

お in front makes it extra polite. You hear it a lot in shops.

Polite

With and without

With a price

このかばんは3000円です。

"This bag is 3000 yen." You already know the price.

With いくら

このかばんはいくらですか？

"How much is this bag?" Swap the price for いくら, add か.

おいくら is the extra polite いくら, common in shops.

いくら + だった ("was") = "how much was it?". んですか asks for the story.

いくら + 払えば ("if I pay") + いい ("good") = "how much should I pay?".

"How much did you steal?"

いくら + 盗った ("stole") = "how much did you steal?". いくら goes right before the verb.

I'm Taking the Day Off · Episode 2

おいくらですか？

"How much is it?"

お + いくら + ですか: the polite shop question, "how much is it?".

Overprotected Kahoko · Episode 1

あっ、ご苦労さま。おいくら？

N5 Grammar

いくつ

Examples

At a bakery with a friend, looking at the melon pan.

これ、いくつ買う？

"How many of these should we get?"

The answer is a ～つ number: ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ.

Casual

A café worker, holding the sugar.

お砂糖はいくつ入れますか？

"How many sugars would you like?"

いくつ sits right before the verb, no particle, the same spot as a number: ふたつ入れます.

Polite

You crouch down to talk to a little kid.

いくつ？

"How old are you?"

The kid holds up fingers: みっつ! いくつ is the soft way to ask a child's age.

Casual

Chatting with an older neighbour.

失礼ですが、おいくつですか？

"If you don't mind me asking, how old are you?"

お in front makes it polite. This is how you ask an adult.

Polite

Counting chairs before guests arrive.

椅子、いくつある？

"How many chairs are there?"

For people, it's 何人 instead: 何人来る？ "How many people are coming?"

Casual

With and without

With a number

りんごをみっつ買いました。

"I bought three apples." You already know how many.

With いくつ

りんごをいくつ買いましたか？

"How many apples did you buy?" Swap the number for いくつ, add か.

Polite

Border · Episode 5

娘さんは おいくつですか？

"How old is your daughter?"

娘さん ("your daughter") + は + おいくつですか = "how old is your daughter?". The polite age question.

Polite

I'm Taking the Day Off · Episode 8

はい おいくつですか？

"Okay. How old are you?"

おいくつですか = "how old are you?", asked to the person directly.

Casual

I'm Taking the Day Off · Episode 4

今 おいくつ？

"How old are you now?"

今 ("now") + おいくつ with a rising voice. Casual: no ですか, but the polite お stays.

Casual

一体いくつ名前があるの？

"Just how many names do you have?"

いくつ + 名前 ("names") + がある ("there are") = "how many names?". 一体: "just, on earth".

Casual

I'm Taking the Day Off · Episode 4

年は いくつなんだ？

"How old is he?"

年 ("age") + は + いくつ = "how old?". なんだ asks for an explanation.

Polite

Border · Episode 4

おいくつですか？

"How old are they?"

おいくつですか: the polite way to ask someone's age.

Casual

おいくつなの？

"How old are you?"

おいくつ (polite) + なの (casual ending) = "how old are you?". Soft and friendly.

N5 Grammar

何か・誰か・どこか

Teasing Master Takagi-san · Season 3, Episode 3

なんだこれ何かの罠か？

"What is this? Some kind of trap?"

Add か to a question word and it stops being a question: 何 "what" → 何か "something".

Same trick for the others: 誰か "someone", どこか "somewhere". On this card, 何かの罠 = "some kind of trap".

が and を often drop after them: 何か食べる？ Polite: 何かありますか？

Examples

Your friend looks hungry.

何か食べる？

"Want to eat something?"

Answer is just yes or no: うん、食べる.

Casual

A shop assistant, after explaining something.

何か質問はありますか？

"Do you have any questions?"

Polite

You're stuck under a heavy box.

誰か手伝って！

"Someone help!"

Casual

A coworker on Friday.

週末、どこか行きますか？

"Are you going anywhere this weekend?"

Polite

With and without

With 何

何を食べる？

"What will you eat?" A real question, wants a name.

With 何か

何か食べる？

"Want to eat something?" Yes or no is enough.

Polite

YouTube · video

"Someone was negotiating."

誰か = "someone", with が as the subject.

どこかに, not どこに: "somewhere", not "where".

"I'll go buy some dry snacks or something."

何か + a noun = "some ___". No を needed after it.

"Want something to drink?"

何か ("something") + 飲む ("drink") = "want something to drink?". No を after 何か.

何か ("something") + 言って ("say") = "say something!". よ makes it pleading.

何かありましたか？

"Did something happen?"

何か ("something") + ありました ("happened, there was") = "did something happen?".

Polite

The Wind Rises

あと 何かいりますか？

"Do you need anything else?"

あと ("else, more") + 何か + いります ("need") = "do you need anything else?".

N5 Grammar

何も・誰も・どこも

YouTube · Road to Vostok #1

何も持てませんよ。

"I can't carry anything." [My bag is full.]

Add も to a question word and put a negative verb after it: 何も + ません = "nothing, not anything".

Same trick for the others: 誰も "nobody", どこも "nowhere". The verb has to be negative.

Casual: 何も持てない.

Examples

You open the fridge.

何もない。

"There's nothing."

Casual

You call out in an empty office.

誰もいません。

"Nobody's here."

Polite

A friend asks about your weekend.

どこにも行かなかった。

"I didn't go anywhere."

With に, it goes between: どこ + に + も.

Casual

A doctor asks about breakfast.

今朝は何も食べませんでした。

"I didn't eat anything this morning."

Polite

With and without

With 何か

何か食べた？

"Did you eat something?"

With 何も

何も食べなかった。

"I didn't eat anything." も + a negative verb.

Sentence mining

Polite

YouTube · video

あ、ちょっと何もないけど左に曲がりますね。

"Ah, there's nothing here really, but I'll turn left."

何も + ない = "there's nothing".

Polite

YouTube · video

あ、これ何も塩胡椒してないですね。

"Ah, I haven't put any salt or pepper on this."

何も + してない = "haven't done anything (to it)".

Polite

The Journalist · Episode 2

僕は何も知りません。

"I don't know anything."

何も + 知りません ("don't know") = "don't know anything". 何も always comes with a negative.

Polite

Sailor Suit and Machine Gun · Episode 2

何も隠してないですよ。

"We're not hiding anything."

何も + 隠してない ("aren't hiding") = "not hiding anything". よ: telling you so.

Casual

Mob Psycho 100 · Episode 5

僕は何もしてないよ。

"I didn't do anything."

何も + してない ("haven't done") = "haven't done anything".

Casual

I am Mita, Your Housekeeper · Episode 5

誰もいないんだしさ、いいだろ？

"Nobody's here, so it's fine, right?"

誰も + いない ("isn't here") = "nobody's here". 誰も is the "nobody" of 何も.

Casual

Spirited Away

お前、何も覚えてないのか。

"Don't you remember anything?"

何も + 覚えてない ("don't remember") = "don't remember anything". のか: "so you...?".

N5 Grammar

何でも・誰でも・どこでも

YouTube · video

都会の生活は便利、何でもあるし。

"City life is convenient. There's everything [you could want]."

Add でも to a question word and it means "any-": 何でも "anything", 誰でも "anyone", どこでも "anywhere", いつでも "any time".

The verb stays positive. On this card, 何でもある: whatever you name, the city has it.

Works the same in polite speech: 何でもあります.

Examples

A friend asks what you want for dinner.

何でもいいよ。

"Anything's fine."

Casual

A teacher talks about a free event.

誰でも参加できます。

"Anyone can join."

Polite

Someone asks where to sit on a train with free seating.

どこでも座っていいですよ。

"You can sit anywhere."

Polite

Saying bye to a friend at your door.

いつでも来てね。

"Come by any time."

Casual

With and without

With 何も

何も食べない。

"I don't eat anything." も + a negative verb.

With 何でも

何でも食べる。

"I eat anything." でも + a positive verb.

One question word, three endings: 何か "something", 何も "nothing" (with a negative verb), 何でも "anything".

何 + でも = "anything". します ("do") = "I'll do anything".

"Anything is fine."

何でも ("anything") + いい ("fine") = "anything is fine".

何でもない is a fixed phrase: "it's nothing, never mind". Good to know as a whole.

何でも ("anything") + やる ("do") = "I'll do anything". ギャラさえくれれば: "as long as you pay me".

N5 Grammar

も

YouTube · video

クロワッサンも好きです

"I like croissants too."

も means "too, also". It goes right after a noun, in the spot where は, が or を would be: クロワッサン + も + 好きです.

On this card, it answers "anything else?". She already said what she likes, and croissants get added to that list.

も takes the place of は, が and を, so never はも or がも. With に or で it goes after them: 箱根にも, "in Hakone too".

Examples

After a long hike, your friend says they're exhausted.

私も疲れた。

"I'm tired too."

At a bakery, you've picked a melon bun and point at one more.

これもください。

"This one too, please."

It rained all day. You check the forecast.

明日も雨だ。

"Tomorrow's rain too."

With and without

With は

私は行きます。

"I'm going." Just about you.

With も

私も行きます。

"I'm going too." Someone else is already going.

A house tour: one more thing on the list of what's there. も sits where が would be.

ホント　仕事場にもクーラー欲しいよ

"Seriously, I want an AC at work too."

にも: に (at work) + も (too). も sits after the particle.

カフェのエリアもありました。

"There was a café area too."

She's listing what the place had. On top of everything else, a café area too.

今日も１日さんざん高木さんにからかわれたな〜

"Today again, Takagi-san teased me all day."

今日も: today too, just like every other day. Time words with も often mean "again".

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 2

夜桜も綺麗だよ

"The cherry blossoms at night are pretty too."

も takes the place of は: 夜桜も = "night cherry blossoms, too".

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 8

春野菜も　いいよね

"Spring vegetables are nice too, right?"

Same move: thing + も + how you feel about it.

涙目にもなりますよ

"Anyone would tear up."

With に, も goes after it: に + も. It doesn't replace に.

N5 Grammar

と

YouTube · video

ヨーロッパと南米に行きました

"[I] went to Europe and South America."

と joins two nouns into one group: "A and B". It goes between them: ヨーロッパ + と + 南米.

The particle that follows (here に) belongs to the whole pair. On this card, it answers "Went where?": Europe and South America, both of them, that's the full list.

と only joins nouns, never verbs or whole sentences. It's the same in polite and casual speech.

Examples

At the konbini counter, ordering.

おにぎりとお茶をください。

"An onigiri and a tea, please."

A friend asks what's in your camera bag.

カメラとレンズ二本。

"A camera and two lenses."

Telling someone who lives with you.

妻と猫がいます。

"There's my wife and the cat."

The pair takes one が, after the second noun.

With and without

Without

コーヒーをください。

Just one thing: a coffee.

With と

コーヒーとケーキをください。

Two things in one order. を comes once, at the end of the pair.

Works for people too: Pikachu and me, then は for the whole pair.

冬服と夏服両方持ってきました

"I brought both winter and summer clothes."

両方 (both) right after the pair makes it extra clear.

アイドルと学業の両立がね。

"Juggling being an idol and school, huh."

両立 is doing two things at once, so と lists the two things.

ほうじ茶と玄米茶がありますからね

"Because there's hojicha and genmaicha."

Same shape as 妻と猫がいます: the pair, then が.

Casual

道の脇に車とテントが

"By the side of the road, a car and a tent."

The verb (ある) is just left off. You still get the picture.

Polite

オレンジとグリーンの組み合わせが好きみたいです。

"Looks like they like the orange and green combo."

オレンジとグリーン is one unit, then の links it to 組み合わせ.

Casual

PiroPito · First Playthrough of Minecraft #05

ゲームのストーリーと核心。

"The game's story and its core."

Just a list, no verb. と is happy without one.

N5 Grammar

や

NHK News Web Easy · article

外に出るときは、帽子や日傘を使ってください。

"When you go outside, use [things like] a hat or a parasol."

や joins nouns like と does: "A and B". It goes between them: 帽子 + や + 日傘.

The difference: と is the full list, や is just a few examples. On this card: hat, parasol, that kind of thing. A cap or a towel would be fine too.

Often など ("and so on") comes after the last noun to make that clear. It only joins nouns, and it's the same in polite and casual speech.

Examples

A friend asks what you had at the izakaya.

焼き鳥や枝豆を食べた。

"I had yakitori, edamame, stuff like that."

Telling a guest what's in the fridge.

ビールやお茶などがあります。

"There's beer, tea and so on."

など after the last noun: "and other things too".

Talking about your weekends.

週末は公園やカフェに行きます。

"On weekends I go to places like the park or a café."

The particle (に) comes once, after the last noun, same as with と.

With and without

With と

ペンとノートを買いました。

I bought a pen and a notebook. That's it, nothing else.

With や

ペンやノートを買いました。

I bought pens, notebooks, that sort of stuff. There was probably more in the bag.

N5 Grammar

か (Or)

YouTube · video

みなさんが日本に来る時は成田空港か羽田空港に到着すると思います。

"When you come to Japan, I think you'll arrive at Narita Airport or Haneda Airport."

か between two nouns means or: A か B, "A or B". It's one of them, not both.

On this card, she answers "Which airport will I land at?": 成田空港 + か + 羽田空港. The particle for the pair (に) comes after the second one.

Same in polite and casual. Between two nouns か is "or"; at the very end of a sentence it's the question か.

Examples

A coworker wants to set up a meeting.

明日か明後日、時間ありますか？

"Do you have time tomorrow or the day after?"

Two か here: the first is "or", the last one makes it a question.

Polite

The clerk at the register.

現金かカード、どちらにしますか？

"Cash or card, which will it be?"

Polite

You and a friend can't decide on dinner.

ラーメンかカレーにしよう。

"Let's go with ramen or curry."

Either is fine, you'll pick one of the two.

Casual

Your friend asks when you're free.

土曜日か日曜日なら大丈夫。

"Saturday or Sunday works."

Casual

With and without

With と

ラーメンとカレーを食べた。

"I ate ramen and curry." Both of them. (See と.)

With か

ラーメンかカレーを食べる。

"I'll eat ramen or curry." Just one of them.

Without

雨が降りそうです。

"It looks like rain." Only rain.

With か

雨か雪が降りそうです。

"It looks like rain or snow." Not sure which.

ドア ("door") + か + 何か ("something") = "a door or something". Handy when you're not sure what it is.

N5 Grammar

が

Source unknown

桜が満開です

"The cherry blossoms are in full bloom."

が marks who or what does something or is in some state, when that's new information. It goes right after the noun: 桜 + が + 満開です.

On this card, you notice something new: the blossoms are out. The sentence answers "What's happening?", and が presents 桜 as the news.

With は (桜は満開です) it would mean "as for the cherry blossoms, they're in full bloom": talking about blossoms you were already discussing, not announcing them.

Examples

Someone at an exhibition asks who made this illustration.

私が描きました。

"I drew it." (me, the one standing here)

You look out the window and notice something.

あ、雨が降ってる！

"Oh, it's raining!"

A friend asks what kind of animals you like.

猫が好き。

"I like cats."

は or が?

With は

私はセブです。

Introducing yourself. "Me? I'm Seb."

With が

私がセブです。

A client looks around asking "which one is Seb?" You raise your hand: "I'm Seb."

N5 Grammar

を

Source unknown

炭酸水を買います

"[I'll] buy sparkling water."

を marks the object: the thing the action is done to. It goes right after that noun, before the verb: 炭酸水 + を + 買います.

On this card, 買います is "buy", and を tells you what gets bought. It answers "Buy what?": sparkling water. There's no "I": it's clear who's buying, so Japanese leaves it out (the [brackets]).

Written を, said "o". In casual speech it's often dropped: 炭酸水買う.

Examples

A friend texts asking what you're up to.

表紙を描いてる。

"Drawing a cover."

At the konbini counter.

コーヒーをください。

"A coffee, please."

Walking the beach in Chigasaki with your camera.

海の写真を撮る。

"I'm taking photos of the sea."

With and without

With を

コーヒーを飲みますか？

Polite, complete. Shops, clients.

Dropped

コーヒー飲む？

With friends を often just disappears. Totally fine.

を marks what is being asked for: the order.

Who are we calling? The aerobics lady, so を.

N5 Grammar

に

YouTube · video

サッカー場に着きました。

"[Here we are,] we've arrived at the soccer field."

に marks a point: the place you end up, the place something is, or the time something happens. It goes right after that place or time: サッカー場 + に + 着く.

On this card, 着く is "arrive", and に tells you where you land. It answers "Arrived where?": at the soccer field.

Same in polite and casual speech. Moving to a place (行く, 来る, 帰る, 着く) takes に, and so does just being there (いる, ある). Doing an action there takes で instead.

Examples

A friend asks about your plans for Saturday.

鎌倉に行く。

"I'm going to Kamakura."

Where are you headed? Kamakura, so に.

Your partner can't find the keys.

鍵は机の上にあるよ。

"The keys are on the desk."

Nothing is happening, the keys are just there. ある and いる take に.

Setting up a call with a coworker.

3時に電話します。

"I'll call at 3."

A clock time is a point too, so it gets に. Words like 今日 or 明日 don't take it: 明日電話します.

With and without

で: doing something there

公園で遊ぶ。

"I play in the park." There's an action (遊ぶ), so the place gets で.

に: going there or being there

公園にいる。

"I'm in the park." No action, you just are there. Same with 公園に行く, "I'm going to the park".

へ

How do you like Wednesday? · Episode 1

深夜バス、オレンジライナー、東京から西へ約900キロ。

"The overnight bus, the Orange Liner, [heading] about 900 km west from Tokyo."

へ (said "e") marks the direction something moves in: toward. It goes right after a place or a direction word: 西 + へ.

On this card, there's no verb at all, and へ still tells you the bus is on its way somewhere. It answers "Heading which way?": west.

Same in polite and casual speech. With 行く, 来る, 帰る you can use へ or に: へ leans on the direction, に on the spot you land.

Examples

Leaving the office, a coworker asks where you're off to.

駅へ行きます。

"I'm heading to the station."

駅に行きます means the same thing. With 行く, either one is fine.

Watching birds fly over in autumn.

鳥が南へ飛んでいく。

"The birds are flying south."

No destination, just a direction. That's へ's home turf.

It's late, and the party is winding down.

そろそろ家へ帰ろう。

"Let's head home soon."

家へ帰る: going back toward home. 家に帰ろう works too.

You thought you were meeting at the station, but your friend texts "I'll come to your place tonight."

ここへ？

"[You're coming] here?"

The verb (来るの) is dropped because it's obvious. へ alone says "coming this way". Just ここ？ could mean anything.

With and without

に: the spot you land

京都に着いた。

"I arrived in Kyoto." The point is that you're there now.

へ: the way you're going

京都へ向かった。

"I headed for Kyoto." The point is the direction. You might still be on the way.

"Last time, I built a house by the sea, a little way south of the outpost."

南へ行った: "went south". A direction word, so へ fits naturally.

"Local shows, like in Hokkaido, have all kinds of 'let's go somewhere' guides... in Japan, abroad, tourist spots."

"When you drive somewhere it snows, get winter tyres and chains ready and drive carefully."

雪が降る所 is "a place where it snows", and へ points the trip there.

"Where do you think you're going?"

どこ + へ ("to") + 行く ("go") = "where are you going?". つもりなんだ: "do you think", a bit threatening.

"Where did they go?"

どこ + へ + 行った ("went") = "where did they go?". ヤツら: "those guys", rough.

こっち ("this way") + へ + 行こう ("let's go"). へ points the direction.

Casual

"Are you going to the valley now?"

中折れ谷 (a valley's name) + へ + 行く = "going to the valley". の？ makes it a casual question.

Entry "e" (へ) · pp. 116–117

N5 Grammar

で

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 1

もう外でダラダラしよっと

"[Forget it,] I'll just go laze around outside."

で marks the place where an action happens. It goes right after the place, before the action: 外 + で + ダラダラする.

On this card, ダラダラする is "laze around", and で tells you where. It answers "Do it where?": outside.

Same in polite and casual speech. One thing to watch: for just being somewhere (いる, ある) Japanese uses に, not で: 外にいる, "I'm outside".

Examples

A friend asks where you usually work on your drawings.

カフェで描いてる。

"I draw at a café."

Telling a coworker about your lunch.

コンビニでおにぎりを買いました。

"I bought an onigiri at the konbini."

Where did I buy it? At the konbini, so で. What did I buy? The onigiri, so を.

Planning a summer weekend in Chigasaki.

海で泳ごう！

"Let's swim in the sea!"

With and without

に: just being there

図書館にいる。

"I'm at the library." Nobody is doing anything, you just are there. いる and ある take に.

で: doing something there

図書館で勉強する。

"I study at the library." There's an action (勉強する), so the place gets で.

N5 Grammar

で (Means)

YouTube · video

箕面市は電車で来ることができます。

"You can get to Minoh City by train."

で after a thing says what you use to do something: by, with, in. 電車 + で = by train. 箸で (with chopsticks), 日本語で (in Japanese) work the same way.

On this card, the sentence answers "How do I get there?": by train.

It's the same で as "at a place" (家で, at home), only here it comes after a tool, a vehicle or a language. で never changes; polite or casual shows at the end.

Examples

A friend asks how you get to work.

自転車で行く。

"I go by bike."

Casual

At a restaurant, the waiter offers you a fork.

大丈夫です、箸で食べます。

"It's okay, I'll eat with chopsticks."

Polite

At the register, your friend asks if you're paying cash.

ううん、カードで払う。

"No, I'll pay by card."

Casual

The teacher asks if you wrote your essay in English.

いいえ、日本語で書きました。

"No, I wrote it in Japanese."

Polite

With and without

Plain

東京に行きます。

"I'm going to Tokyo."

With で

新幹線で東京に行きます。

"I'm going to Tokyo by shinkansen." で says how.

With で

箸で食べます。

"I eat with chopsticks." The chopsticks are the tool.

Not this

箸を食べます。

"I eat chopsticks." を makes them the food.

N5 Grammar

と (With)

YouTube · video

僕は旅行する時に、地元の人と話したいです。

"When I travel, I want to talk with the local people."

と after a person means "with": the person you do the action together with. It goes right after them: 地元の人 + と.

On this card, it answers "With who?": talk with the locals. Then the verb comes later.

Between two nouns と means "and" (ヨーロッパと南米). With a verb after it, it's "with". Same in polite and casual speech.

Examples

Someone asks who you went to the concert with.

姉と行った。

"I went with my sister."

Saturday plans.

友達と映画を見ます。

"I'm watching a movie with a friend."

Asking a coworker to lunch.

私と一緒に食べませんか？

"Want to eat with me?"

一緒に (together) after と makes the "with" extra clear. Very common.

With and without

Without

京都に行きました。

I went to Kyoto. Maybe alone, we don't know.

With と

母と京都に行きました。

I went to Kyoto with my mom. Now we know who came along.

じいじ ("Grandpa") + と + 一緒にいる ("be together") + と ("when") = "when she's with Grandpa".

N5 Grammar

と (Quotation)

Polite～と思います
Casual～と思う neutral
～って思う spoken, very common

Same meaning: quoting a thought. って is the spoken casual と.

Polite

YouTube · video

そうですね！本当に、みんなのおかげだと思います！

"Totally! I think it's really all thanks to everyone!"

と closes off what someone thinks or says. The thought goes first, then と, then 思う (think) or 言う (say): みんなのおかげだ + と + 思います.

On this card, it answers "What do you think?": that it's all thanks to everyone. After a noun or な-adjective, add だ before と (おかげだと). After a verb or い-adjective, just と (高いと思う).

と works in polite and casual speech. In casual talk it often turns into って (below).

Casual

YouTube · video

でも、なんか日本人で、すごくありそうな考え方だなって思いました。

"But I thought, that's such a Japanese way of thinking."

って is the casual と. Same job, same spot: thought + って + 思う. The thought here is 考え方だな, "what a (Japanese) way of thinking".

Examples

A friend asks about the new ramen place.

おいしいと思う。

"I think it's good."

Passing on what the teacher said.

先生は、明日テストがあると言いました。

"The teacher said there's a test tomorrow."

What was said goes before と, who said it goes up front with は.

Looking at dark clouds.

明日は雨だと思います。

"I think it'll rain tomorrow."

雨 is a noun, so だ comes before と. Same with な-adjectives: 静かだと思う.

Telling a friend why Tanaka-san isn't here.

田中さん、来ないって言ってたよ。

"Tanaka-san said they're not coming."

Casual: って instead of と.

With and without

Without

雨です。

It's raining. A plain fact.

With と

雨だと思います。

I think it's raining. Now it's just my guess: と wraps up "it's rain", 思います says I think it.

コンタクトなんか怖いって言ってたのに

言ってた: "you were saying". のに adds "and yet (look at you now)".

N5 Grammar

の (Possession)

YouTube · video

名古屋は僕の地元です。

"Nagoya is my hometown."

の links two nouns: the owner first, then the thing. 僕 + の + 地元: my hometown. Like "'s" in English, but always in that order.

On this card, it answers "Whose hometown?": mine. Without の, 僕 and 地元 would just sit next to each other with no link.

The same in polite and casual speech. 私の, 僕の, 俺の are simply how you say "my".

Examples

Showing a friend a photo on your phone.

これ、僕の犬。

"This is my dog."

Casual

An umbrella is left by the door at work.

これは田中さんの傘ですか？

"Is this Tanaka-san's umbrella?"

Polite

Telling someone where you're eating tonight.

友達のお母さんの店に行く。

"I'm going to my friend's mom's shop."

You can chain の, just like 's 's in English.

Casual

With and without

Without

車です。

"It's a car." Just what it is.

With の

僕の車です。

"It's my car." Now you know whose.

N5 Grammar

から

Polite

Comprehensible Japanese · これ、それ、あれ、どれ

松ぼっくりは、松の木からおちます。

"Pine cones fall from pine trees."

から means from. It marks the starting point, and it goes right after it: 松の木 + から = "from the pine tree".

On this card, the pine cone starts up in the tree and ends on the ground. The sentence answers "Where do they fall from?": the tree.

から is the same in polite and casual speech. The politeness comes from the end: おちます here, おちる with friends.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 6

昔から、マイペースだよな、お前は

"You've always done things at your own pace, haven't you."

から works for time too: 昔 + から = "from long ago", so "always". Casual, so だよな instead of ですね.

Examples

A new coworker asks where you're from.

ドイツから来ました。

"I came from Germany."

Place + から: where you started.

Polite

Someone asks when the shop opens.

十時からです。

"From ten o'clock."

Time + から: when something starts.

Polite

Your friend shows you a new sweater.

お母さんからもらった。

"I got it from my mom."

Person + から: who it came from.

Casual

You're about to start cleaning a messy room.

どこからやろう？

"Where should I start?"

Literally "from where should I do it?"

Casual

With and without

Without

駅に歩きました。

"I walked to the station." The station is where you ended up.

With から

駅から歩きました。

"I walked from the station." The station is where you started.

N5 Grammar

まで

Polite

YouTube · video

でも、昔の侍は東京から京都まで歩いたらしいです。

"But back then, samurai apparently walked all the way from Tokyo to Kyoto."

まで means until, up to, as far as. It marks the end point, and it goes right after it: 京都 + まで = "as far as Kyoto".

It often teams up with から (from): 東京から京都まで = "from Tokyo to Kyoto". On this card, the sentence answers "How far did they walk?": all the way to Kyoto.

まで is the same in polite and casual speech. The politeness comes from the end: らしいです here, らしい with friends.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 1

何時まで寝てるの

"How long are you going to sleep?"

まで works for time too: 何時 + まで = "until when". Casual, so just の at the end instead of んですか.

Examples

A friend asks about your work hours.

九時から五時まで働きます。

"I work from nine to five."

Time + まで: when something stops.

Polite

The bus isn't coming and the station is close.

駅まで歩こう。

"Let's walk to the station."

Place + まで: how far you go.

Casual

Your friend is still finishing their homework.

終わるまで待つよ。

"I'll wait until you're done."

Verb (dictionary form) + まで: until that thing happens.

Casual

Your joke was so silly that the strict teacher laughed too.

先生まで笑った！

"Even the teacher laughed!"

Person or thing + まで can also mean even: it goes "as far as" the one you'd least expect.

Casual

With and without

Without

七時に寝ます。

"I go to sleep at seven." に is one point in time: when it starts.

With まで

七時まで寝ます。

"I sleep until seven." まで is where the sleeping ends.

最後まで 一緒にいたい。

"I want to be with you until the end."

最後 ("the end") + まで = "until the end". 一緒にいたい: "I want to be together".

最後 ("the end") + まで + 信じて ("believe") = "believe me to the end". くれないか: "won't you?".

N5 Grammar

だけ

Polite

YouTube · video

夢応援面談　聞くのは３つだけです

"The Dream Support Interview: I only ask three questions."

だけ means only, just. It goes right after the thing you're limiting: ３つ + だけ = "only three".

On this card: no fourth question, no follow-ups. He's saying it's that simple. It answers "How many questions?": just three.

だけ is the same in polite and casual speech. The politeness comes from the end: だけです here, just だけ with friends.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 5

間違いはないけど、フェアなのに定番だけじゃつまらない。

"They're a safe choice, but for a special menu, [having] only the usual ones is boring."

定番 + だけ = "only the usual ones". Casual, so no です at the end.

Examples

At the café, the waiter asks what you'd like.

コーヒーだけお願いします。

"Just a coffee, please."

Noun + だけ. No cake, no sandwich, only coffee.

Polite

Someone asks if you speak lots of languages.

英語と日本語だけです。

"Only English and Japanese."

だけ can cover a whole list: 英語と日本語 + だけ.

Polite

Your friend offers you more snacks.

一個だけちょうだい。

"Just give me one."

Number + だけ: only one, not more.

Casual

Your friend asks what you did on Sunday.

家で寝てただけ。

"I just slept at home."

Verb + だけ: that's all you did. The verb stays in its plain form (寝てた, 見る, 行った).

Casual

With and without

Without

水を飲みました。

"I drank water." Maybe you had other things too.

With だけ

水だけ飲みました。

"I only drank water." Nothing else. を often drops out after だけ.

Polite

でも、昔のキンドルは少しだけ凹んでいます。

"But on the old Kindle, the screen is just a little sunken in."

少し + だけ = "just a little". だけ makes 少し even smaller.

"That's just going to car 0 and hitting the brakes in the driver's cab past it."

Verb + だけ: that's all there is to do. ブレーキをかけるだけ = "just put on the brakes".

"That's it?"

それ ("that") + だけ = "only that?". Said when you expected more.

"All that's left is to hand it in."

あとは ("the rest is") + 出す ("hand in") + だけ: the only thing left is to hand it in.

悲しい ("sad") + だけ = "just sad", nothing else. ただ adds "simply".

N5 Grammar

しか～ない

Casual

YouTube · video

教授の実験の手伝いでさ、3時間しか寝てねえ。

"I was helping the professor with his experiment, so I only got three hours of sleep."

しか means only, but the verb after it is always negative. It goes right after the thing you're limiting: 3時間 + しか.

On this card, 3時間しか寝てない is "I didn't sleep anything but three hours". It answers "How much did you sleep?": not enough. ねえ is a rough, casual way to say ない.

しか always sounds like "that's all, and it's not much". In polite speech the end becomes ません: しか寝ていません.

Polite

YouTube · video

これサンピン茶は沖縄でしか飲むことができません。ま、多分名古屋にもあるかな。

"This here, sanpin tea, you can only drink in Okinawa. Well, maybe Nagoya has it too."

Polite, so the negative is ません. Place + で + しか: "only in Okinawa". で stays, but を and が drop out before しか.

Examples

You check your wallet before paying.

500円しかありません。

"I only have 500 yen."

Not much money, and you're a bit worried. しか + ありません.

Polite

A coworker asks if you speak Chinese too.

日本語と英語しか話せません。

"I can only speak Japanese and English."

しか can cover a whole list: 日本語と英語 + しか.

Polite

Your friend opens your fridge, looking for food.

ビールしかないよ。

"There's nothing but beer."

ビールがない would be "there's no beer". With しか it flips: beer is the only thing there.

Casual

Your friend asks how many people came to the party.

三人しか来なかった。

"Only three people came."

Past: しか + なかった. You hoped for more.

Casual

With and without

Without

三時間寝た。

"I slept three hours." Just a fact.

With しか

三時間しか寝てない。

"I only slept three hours." Not enough, and you feel it. Same as だけ in meaning, but だけ is neutral (三時間だけ寝た) and しか sounds like a complaint.

パンダ君の好物しかおいてないじゃない..　そのカフェ。

"That café only has Panda's favorite foods, doesn't it..."

しか + おいてない (置いてない, "don't keep"). The じゃない at the end is "isn't it?", not part of しか.

世界に４枚しかないうちの１枚じゃ、値段のつけようもないわい。

"It's one of only four in the world, so there's no way to put a price on it."

４枚しかない = "there are only four". Here it describes the cards: "the only-four-in-the-world ones".

君しかいないんだ。

"You're the only one."

君 ("you") + しか + いない ("isn't there") = "there's nobody but you", "you're the only one".

"So you can only use it on weekdays?"

平日 ("weekdays") + しか + 使えない ("can't use") = "can only use it on weekdays".

信じるしかないな。

"All we can do is trust her."

信じる ("believe") + しかない = "nothing to do but believe". Verb + しかない: it's the only option left.

Casual

Overprotected Kahoko · Episode 2

加穂子にしかできないこと

"Something only Kahoko can do."

加穂子 + に ("for") + しか + できない ("can't do") = "something only Kahoko can do".

Casual

仲直りするしかないよ。

"We just have to make up."

仲直りする ("make up") + しかない = "we have no choice but to make up".

N5 Grammar

ぐらい・くらい

Polite

YouTube · video

フレーバーの紅茶で、100種類ぐらいあるんですよ！

"There are about 100 kinds of flavored tea!"

ぐらい means about, roughly. It goes right after an amount: 100種類 + ぐらい = "about 100 kinds".

On this card, she didn't count them. ぐらい tells you the number is a rough guess. It answers "How many?": around 100.

くらい and ぐらい are the same word. Say whichever comes out, both are fine in polite and casual speech.

Casual

YouTube · video

最初の1時間は無料なんだけど、それ以降は1時間100円くらい。

"The first hour is free, but after that it's about 100 yen an hour."

Same thing with くらい: 100円くらい = "about 100 yen". Casual, so no です at the end.

Examples

Someone asks how long you've studied Japanese.

3年ぐらいです。

"About three years."

Without ぐらい it's exactly three years. With it, "give or take".

Polite

Asking the hotel how far the station is.

駅まで歩いてどのくらいかかりますか？

"How long does it take to walk to the station?"

どの + くらい = "about how much?": the question version. どれくらい means the same. Answer: 10分ぐらいです.

Polite

Your friend is cooking rice and asks you.

ご飯、どれくらい食べる？

"How much rice do you want?"

You can answer with your hands: このくらい. "About this much."

Casual

A friend asks how much your new bike cost.

5万円くらいかな。

"About 50,000 yen, I think."

くらい + かな: you're not quite sure of the price.

Casual

With and without

Without

駅まで10分かかります。

"It takes 10 minutes to the station." Sounds exact.

With ぐらい

駅まで10分ぐらいかかります。

"It takes about 10 minutes to the station." A rough guess.

モントリオールから、車で１時間ぐらいのところです。

"It's a place about an hour by car from Montreal."

1時間ぐらいのところ: "a place about an hour away". ぐらい + の before a noun.

Casual

YouTube · video

ちょっと雪も降りました。ちょっとね。このぐらいかな。

"It snowed a little too. Just a bit. About this much, I guess."

このぐらい: "about this much", while showing it. Polite start, casual かな at the end.

"Around 35 or so."

35とか ("35 or so") + それ ("that") + ぐらい = "around that". Two ways of saying "roughly" at once.

Casual

Steins Gate · Episode 1

15分くらい前。

"About fifteen minutes ago."

15分 ("15 minutes") + くらい + 前 ("ago") = "about 15 minutes ago".

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 15

20回くらい。

"About twenty times."

20回 ("20 times") + くらい = "about twenty times".

Polite

40分 ("40 minutes") + くらい + でしょうか ("I'd say"): a polite guess.

N5 Grammar

ごろ (頃)

Midnight Diner (深夜食堂) · opening

営業時間は夜12時から、朝7時ごろまで。

"My hours are from midnight until about seven in the morning." [the diner's opening hours]

ごろ means around, about, for a point in time. It goes right after the time: 7時 + ごろ = "around 7 o'clock".

On this card, midnight is a fixed time, so no ごろ. Seven is a rough end time, so it gets ごろ. It answers "When?": around seven.

Same word in polite and casual speech. In writing you'll also see it as 頃.

Examples

A coworker asks when you'll get to the office.

9時ごろ着きます。

"I'll get there around nine."

Some people add に: 9時ごろに着きます. Same meaning, with or without it.

Polite

Your friend asks when you went to bed.

2時ごろかな。

"Around two, I think."

Casual

Talking about when the cherry blossoms come out.

桜は4月の初めごろです。

"The cherry blossoms are around early April."

Not only clock times: days, months and seasons work too.

Polite

Planning when to meet up.

じゃあ、6時ごろ駅で。

"Okay, at the station around six, then."

Casual

With and without

Without

7時に起きました。

"I got up at seven." Sounds exact.

With ごろ

7時ごろ起きました。

"I got up around seven." A rough time.

ごろ or ぐらい?

ぐらい: how long

2時間ぐらい寝ました。

"I slept for about two hours." An amount of time.

ごろ: when

2時ごろ寝ました。

"I went to bed around two." A point in time.

午後11時 ("11 p.m.") + ごろ = "around 11 p.m.". 昨日の: "yesterday's".

"Around what time is Shinkai coming?"

何時 ("what time") + ごろ = "around what time?".

"From around 12 to around 5."

ごろ works with から and まで too.

Polite

症状が出始めたのは いつごろですか？

"Around when did the symptoms start?"

いつ ("when") + ごろ = "around when?". 症状が出始めた: "the symptoms started".

Casual

今日 帰り何時ごろ？

"Around what time are you coming home today?"

何時 ("what time") + ごろ = "around what time?". 帰り: "coming home". Casual: no です.

うん、3時ごろかな。

"Yeah, around 3, I think."

3時 ("3 o'clock") + ごろ = "around 3". かな: "I think".

N5 Grammar

よ

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 8

取材の人ですよ

"[Those people?] They're here for an interview, you know."

よ at the end of a sentence means "I'm telling you something you don't know yet". It goes on the very end, after です, ます or a plain verb or adjective.

On this card, the other person doesn't know who the visitors are. The speaker fills them in. Without よ, 取材の人です is just a flat fact; with よ it's "hey, here's the info you're missing".

Polite: ですよ / ますよ. Casual: drop です, but after a noun or な-adjective add だ: 取材の人だよ.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 2

お花見らしくなってきたよ

"It's starting to look like a real hanami party!"

Here よ goes right after the plain verb. They're hanging up flags and sharing how it's coming along with everyone around them.

Examples

Your friend is about to leave without their phone. It's still on the table.

スマホ、忘れてるよ

"You're forgetting your phone!"

Casual

Your friend is trying to decide if the new ramen place is worth it. You've been.

あそこ、おいしいよ

"That place is good, trust me."

Casual

A customer is looking around for the bathroom. You work there.

トイレは二階ですよ

"The bathroom's upstairs."

Polite

A coworker is rushing to catch the 6:00 train. You know it was cancelled.

その電車、今日は来ませんよ

"That train isn't coming today, just so you know."

Polite

With and without

Without

おいしい

"It's tasty." You're eating and just say it, to yourself or anyone.

With よ

おいしいよ

"It's tasty, try it!" You're telling someone who hasn't tried it.

Without

二階です

"It's on the second floor." Neutral answer.

With よ

二階ですよ

"It's upstairs." Friendlier, you're helping them out.

Telling the viewer something they might not know. よ after です.

Polite

"If you don't want people reading it, you should make it private."

Advice is a classic place for よ: you're handing over a tip they hadn't thought of.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 3

僕だってね、アリばっかり食べたくないよ

"Hey, I don't want to eat nothing but ants either!"

Everyone assumes he loves ants. He's setting them straight. よ after the plain negative ない.

Casual
