刻んだ竹が口に刺さりそうだよ

"The chopped bamboo looks like it'll stab me in the mouth!"

He's telling the others about a problem only he can feel. そう ("looks like") works like a な-adjective, so casual gets だよ.

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 4

食べ放題ですよ

"It's all you can eat!"

Telling them something they don't know yet. Polite: ですよ.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 21

デスクワークだよ。

"It's desk work."

デスクワーク ("desk work") + だよ. Casual だ + よ: correcting someone who guessed wrong.

Casual

"Believe me."

信じて ("believe me") + よ: a て-form request with よ sounds pushy, "come on, believe me".

N5 Grammar

ね

Polite

YouTube · video

綺麗な鳴き声ですね

"[Hear that bird?] What a beautiful song, isn't it?"

ね at the end of a sentence means "you see it too, right?". It goes on the very end, after です, ます or a plain verb or adjective.

On this card, she's walking in the forest with her viewers, and they can all hear the bird. She isn't giving news, she's sharing the moment and inviting them to agree.

Polite: ですね / ますね. Casual: drop です, but after a noun or な-adjective add だ: 綺麗な鳴き声だね.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 5

楽しそうだね

"That sounds fun, huh."

そう ("looks like") works like a な-adjective, so it gets だ before ね.

Examples

You and a friend step outside. It's freezing.

寒いね

"It's cold, huh."

Casual

You're both eating the curry your friend made. It's really good.

これ、おいしいね

"This is good, isn't it."

Casual

Small talk with a neighbor while it pours outside.

よく降りますね

"It sure is raining a lot."

Polite

A coworker shows you a photo of their new apartment.

広い部屋ですね

"What a big room."

Polite

With and without

Without

寒い

"It's cold." Just a statement, to yourself or anyone.

With ね

寒いね

"It's cold, huh." You both feel it, and you're sharing that.

With よ

寒いよ

"It's cold, you know." They don't know yet, so you tell them (maybe they're about to go out without a coat).

With ね

広い部屋ですね

"What a big room." You're both looking at it.

She's comparing two places and expects the listener to agree. ね after です.

Reacting to what someone just said, and sharing the feeling.

N5 Grammar

よね

Polite

YouTube · video

仙台には、国際空港もありますよね。

"[Talking about Sendai] Sendai has an international airport too, right?"

よね at the end of a sentence means "I'm pretty sure this is true, right?". It goes on the very end, after です, ます or a plain verb or adjective.

On this card, she knows Sendai has an airport, and she's checking that you're with her. It's not news (that's よ) and it's not something you're both looking at right now (that's ね): it's something she already believes and wants a nod on.

Polite: ですよね / ますよね. Casual: drop です, but after a noun or な-adjective add だ: 週二日だよね.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 14

パンダ君のバイトって、週二日だよね。

"Panda's part-time job is two days a week, right?"

He thinks he remembers, and he's double-checking. 週二日 is a noun, so it gets だ before よね.

Examples

You're meeting a friend tomorrow and want to make sure you have the time right.

明日、十時だよね

"Tomorrow's at ten, right?"

Casual

Your friend says they hate waiting in long lines. You feel the same.

わかる。長い列、嫌だよね

"I get it. Long lines are the worst, right?"

Casual

Not checking a fact here: you're agreeing, and saying "everyone feels this, don't they".

You're about to pay at a shop and want to check before you hand over your card.

カード、使えますよね

"I can use a card, right?"

Polite

A coworker mentioned last week they were from Osaka.

田中さん、大阪出身ですよね

"Tanaka-san, you're from Osaka, right?"

Polite

With and without

With よ

明日、十時だよ

"Tomorrow's at ten, you know." You're telling them. They don't know yet.

With よね

明日、十時だよね

"Tomorrow's at ten, right?" You think so, and you're checking with them.

With ね

寒いね

"It's cold, huh." You both feel it right now, and you're sharing that.

With よね

冬の北海道って、寒いよね

"Hokkaido in winter is cold, right?" Not something you feel right now: something you're sure about and want them to agree with.

N5 Grammar

でしょう

Polite

He Who Can't Marry · Episode 1

開業資金はうちの父が貸してくれるでしょう。

"My dad will probably lend [us] the money to start the business."

でしょう means "probably": you think it's true, but you're not 100% sure. It goes at the very end, after a plain verb, an い-adjective, or a noun (no だ before it).

On this card, she answers "Where will the money come from?": her dad, most likely. Without でしょう it would be a sure thing: 貸してくれます, "he'll lend it".

Said with a rising voice, でしょう？ turns into "right?": you're pretty sure and want the other person to agree.

旅行演習したいって言ったのペンギンさんでしょ。

"You're the one who said you wanted to practice traveling, Penguin, right?"

Casual version: the short でしょ. Men and women both use it with friends, mostly for "right?". Here he's reminding Penguin whose idea this was.

Examples

A client asks when the sketches will be done.

金曜日には終わるでしょう。

"They'll probably be done by Friday."

Polite

Someone at the shop asks if the cake is still fresh.

今日中なら大丈夫でしょう。

"It should be fine if you eat it today."

大丈夫 + でしょう, no だ in between.

Polite

Your friend lies on the couch after a long walk.

疲れたでしょ？

"You're tired, right?"

Casual

Your friend can't find their keys.

カバンの中でしょ？

"They're in your bag, right?"

Casual

With and without

Without

明日は雨です。

"It's going to rain tomorrow." Sure, like you already know.

With でしょう

明日は雨でしょう。

"It'll probably rain tomorrow." A guess. What the weather forecast says.

Without

疲れた。

"I'm tired." About you.

With でしょ？

疲れたでしょ？

"You're tired, right?" About them, asking them to agree.

Same でしょうか, used to make you doubt it.

Noun + でしょ？: 約束でしょ？, "it's a promise, right?".

でしょ = "right?" when you're pretty sure. Short spoken form of でしょう.

でしょう。

Reference

A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

Entry "darō" · pp. 100–102

N5 Grammar

だろう

He Who Can't Marry · Episode 1

俺の受け売りだろう？

"That's [just] what I told you, right?"

だろう does the same job as でしょう: "probably", or with a rising voice "right?". It goes at the very end, after a plain verb, an い-adjective, or a noun (no だ before it).

On this card, he's pretty sure where the other guy got that idea, so it's "right?". Said out loud to someone, だろう and the short だろ sound masculine and a bit blunt. Most women, and plenty of men, say でしょ instead.

Two places where だろう is neutral and everyone uses it: "I wonder..." (なんだろう, said to yourself), and writing or inner thoughts.

Examples

You look at the dark clouds and say it to yourself.

明日も雨だろうな。

"It'll probably rain tomorrow too."

Talking to yourself, so it's fine for anyone. な makes it a thought.

Two guys after football practice.

疲れただろ？

"You're tired, right?"

Masculine. A woman would say 疲れたでしょ？

You find a strange box on your doorstep.

これ、なんだろう？

"I wonder what this is."

Question word + だろう: "I wonder". Used by everyone.

Your friend is late and not answering.

どこにいるんだろう。

"I wonder where they are."

With and without

だろ？

疲れただろ？

"You're tired, right?" Masculine, a bit rough.

でしょ？

疲れたでしょ？

Same meaning. Neutral, anyone can say it.

Without

これ、なに？

"What's this?" Asking someone.

With だろう

これ、なんだろう？

"I wonder what this is." Asking yourself, nobody needs to answer.

N5 Grammar

い-Adjective

Politeおいしいです
Casualおいしい

Same meaning: "it's tasty". Only the politeness changes. The adjective itself stays the same.

Casual

YouTube · video

いつもよりおいしい。

"[It's] tastier than usual."

An い-adjective describes something and ends in い: おいしい (tasty), 寒い (cold), 高い (expensive). It can end a sentence just as it is, no だ needed.

On this card, someone tastes it and compares it to normal. いつもより is "than usual". The sentence answers "How is it?".

Polite: add です, おいしいです. Before a noun it goes straight on, no な: おいしいラーメン.

Polite

YouTube · video

セブンの春巻きが1番美味しいです。

"The spring rolls at Seven [Eleven] are the tastiest."

です goes right after the adjective. 1番 is "the most".

Examples

You step outside in August.

暑い！

"It's hot!"

One word is a full sentence. No だ after an い-adjective.

Casual

A shop clerk shows you a bag. You check the price tag.

ちょっと高いですね。

"It's a bit expensive."

Polite

A friend notices your shoes.

新しい靴？

"New shoes?"

新しい goes right before 靴. No な in between.

Casual

Your boss asks what your new teacher is like.

優しい先生です。

"She's a kind teacher."

優しい describes 先生. The です at the end is for the whole sentence.

Polite

With and without

Just the noun

日

"A day." Could be any day.

Before a noun

寒い日

"A cold day." The adjective goes straight in front.

End of sentence

今日は寒いです。

"It's cold today." Drop です for casual: 今日は寒い。

Not this

寒いな日

な is only for な-adjectives (静かな日). An い-adjective never takes it.

N5 Grammar

いい (良い)

Politeいいです
Casualいい

Same meaning: "it's good". Only the politeness changes.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 5

ふーん和のテイストもいいけど

"Hmm, a Japanese style is nice too, but..."

いい means "good" or "nice". It's an い-adjective: put it at the end to say something is good, or right before a noun: いい天気 (good weather).

On this card, he's weighing ideas and likes the Japanese-style one. 和 is "Japanese", テイスト is "taste, style". It answers "Is it good?".

Polite: いいです. Watch out: every other form comes from 良い (よい): よくない (not good), よかった (was good). Never いくない or いかった.

Polite

YouTube · video

やっぱり息が切れるけどいい運動ですね

"I still get out of breath, but it's good exercise."

Here いい sits right before a noun: いい運動, good exercise. The です at the end makes it polite.

Examples

You open the curtains. Blue sky.

いい天気！

"Nice weather!"

いい right before a noun, like any い-adjective. No な needed.

Casual

A friend asks if they can borrow your pen.

いいよ。

"Sure."

Here いい is "okay, fine", not "good".

Casual

A colleague asks how the new office chairs are.

すごくいいです。

"They're really good."

Polite

A friend asks how your knee is after the run.

あんまりよくない。

"Not great."

"Not good" is よくない, never いくない. It comes from 良い.

Casual

With and without

Good

天気がいい。

"The weather's good." Right now, plain and simple.

Not good

天気がよくない。

"The weather's not good." Switches to よ.

Was good

天気がよかった。

"The weather was good." Also よ.

Not this

いくない・いかった

Feels logical, sounds wrong. Only the plain "good" uses いい.

いい ("good") + ですね = "that's nice", "sounds good". Agreeing with an idea.

"Something like that is cool too."

かっこいい (cool) has いい inside, so it plays by the same rules: かっこよくない, かっこよかった.

ま、両親とすごく仲がいいとか

"Well, like, I get along really well with my parents."

仲がいい is "the relationship is good", so "get along well".

準備 is "preparation", so this is literally "Is your prep good?", which is just "Ready?". いい as "okay".

N5 Grammar

な-Adjective

Politeきれいです
Casualきれいだ plain statement
きれい just the word, very common

Same meaning: "it's pretty". Before a noun it's always な: きれいな夜景.

Polite

YouTube · video

ここが上高地で一番有名な場所です。

"This is the most famous spot in Kamikochi."

A な-adjective is a describing word like 有名 (famous), 静か (quiet), きれい (pretty). When it sits right before a noun, you add な in between: 有名 + な + 場所.

On this card, a vlogger walks up to the river and the bridge. The adjective answers "What kind of place is this?": the most famous one. 一番 is "the most".

The な only shows up before a noun. At the end of a sentence it's gone (see the next card).

Polite

YouTube · video

ここ、夜景がきれいです。

"The night view here is pretty."

Here きれい ends the sentence, so no な: just きれいです. Before a noun it would be きれいな夜景. Casual: きれいだ, or just きれい. Careful: きれい ends in い, but it's a な-adjective.

Examples

A friend asks what your studio in Chigasaki is like.

静かな部屋です。

"It's a quiet room."

静か comes before 部屋, so な goes in between.

Polite

The same friend stays over and notices how quiet it is at night.

静かだね。

"It's quiet, huh."

Same word, end of the sentence, so no な. だ is the casual です.

Casual

Someone asks about your favorite food.

好きな食べ物はカレー。

"My favorite food is curry."

好き looks like a verb in English ("to like"), but it's a な-adjective: 好き + な + 食べ物.

Casual

You trip on the stairs. A coworker rushes over.

大丈夫です。

"I'm okay."

Nothing comes after 大丈夫 but です, so no な.

Polite

With and without

Before a noun

静かな町

"A quiet town." な connects the adjective to the noun.

End of sentence

この町は静かです。

"This town is quiet." No な. Casual: 静かだ, or just 静か.

い-adjective

寒い日

"A cold day." い-adjectives go straight before the noun, no な.

Not this

静か町 · 静かなです

No な before a noun, or な at the end. Both are wrong.

N5 Grammar

い-Adjective (Negative)

YouTube · video

じゃあ、あんまり名古屋詳しくない。

"Well, [then] I don't really know Nagoya that well."

To say something is not a certain way, swap the last い of an い-adjective for くない: 詳しい (knows well) → 詳しくない (doesn't know well).

On this card, the speaker just worked out they've barely spent time in Nagoya. あんまり + くない is "not very". It answers "Do you know Nagoya?".

Polite: 詳しくないです. Watch out: いい becomes よくない, never いくない.

Examples

A friend worries the hike will be too much for you.

大丈夫、そんなに遠くないよ。

"It's fine, it's not that far."

Casual

The shop clerk asks if the coat is too heavy.

いえ、全然重くないです。

"No, it's not heavy at all."

For polite, just put です after くない.

Polite

Someone offers you the spicy curry. You try it.

あれ、辛くない。

"Huh, it's not spicy."

Casual

A coworker asks how you're feeling today.

ちょっと調子がよくないです。

"I'm not feeling great."

いい is the odd one. It turns into よくない, never いくない.

Polite

With and without

Is

高い。

"It's expensive."

Isn't

高くない。

"It's not expensive." Drop the い, add くない.

Polite

高くないです。

Same thing, polite. Also fine: 高くありません, a bit stiffer.

Not this

高いじゃない。

じゃない is for nouns and な-adjectives. い-adjectives use くない.

N5 Grammar

い-Adjective (Past)

Polite良かったです
Casual良かった

Same meaning: "it was good". Only the politeness changes.

Casual

Source unknown

それなら良かった！

"Oh, in that case, I'm glad!"

To say how something was, swap the last い of an い-adjective for かった: 良い (good) → 良かった (was good).

On this card, someone just explained that things turned out fine. 良かった is literally "it was good", and it's how Japanese says "I'm glad". それなら is "in that case". It answers "How did it turn out?".

Polite: 良かったです. Never 良いでした: the past is already in かった. Watch out: いい also becomes 良かった, never いかった.

Polite

Source unknown

めっちゃ気持ちよかったです。

"It felt really good."

Just add です after かった. And again いい turns into よかった: 気持ちいい (feels good) → 気持ちよかった.

Examples

A friend asks how your trip to Hokkaido was.

寒かった！

"It was cold!"

Casual

You leave a ramen place, still full.

おいしかったね。

"That was good, huh."

Casual

A colleague asks about the movie you saw at the weekend.

面白かったです。

"It was interesting."

For polite, just put です after かった. Not 面白いでした.

Polite

A friend asks how the concert was.

よかったよ。

"It was good."

いい is the odd one. It turns into よかった, never いかった.

Casual

With and without

Now

寒い。

"It's cold." You're standing in it right now.

Was

寒かった。

"It was cold." You're home now, telling the story.

Polite

寒かったです。

かった does the past, です just adds politeness.

Not this

寒いでした。

Feels logical, sounds wrong. です never carries the past here.

相手が よくなかった。

"You picked the wrong opponent."

相手 ("opponent") + が + よくなかった ("wasn't good") = "you picked the wrong opponent". いい → よくなかった.

Casual

I am Mita, Your Housekeeper · Episode 2

痛くなかった？

"Didn't it hurt?"

痛い ("painful") → 痛くない → 痛くなかった = "didn't hurt". Rising voice: "didn't it hurt?".

Casual

Million Yen Woman · Episode 1

おいしくなかった？

"Was it not good?"

おいしい ("tasty") → おいしくなかった = "wasn't tasty". Rising voice makes it a question.

Casual

Frieren Beyond Journey's End · Episode 4

もしかして あまり楽しくなかった？

"Could it be you didn't enjoy it much?"

あまり ("not very") + 楽しくなかった ("wasn't fun") = "wasn't much fun". もしかして: "could it be...".

Casual

Fullmetal Alchemist Brotherhood · Episode 23

貴様のトラップ、悪くなかった。

"Your trap wasn't bad."

悪い ("bad") → 悪くなかった = "wasn't bad", a grudging bit of praise. 貴様: a very rough "you".

Casual

From the New World · Episode 10

あの猫だって 別に悪くなかったんだ。

"Even that cat did nothing wrong."

悪い ("bad") → 悪くなかった = "did nothing wrong". あの猫だって: "even that cat".

N5 Grammar

な-Adjective (Negative)

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 4

ちっとも便利じゃないわねスマホ

"Smartphones aren't handy at all, are they?"

To say a な-adjective is not, add じゃない right after it, no な: 便利 (handy) → 便利じゃない. It works exactly like a noun: 学生じゃない.

On this card, the speaker is fed up with her phone. The sentence answers "Are smartphones handy?": not one bit. ちっとも is "not at all", and わね is a soft "aren't they".

Polite: 便利じゃないです, or a bit stiffer 便利じゃありません. Watch out: 綺麗 and 嫌い end in い but are な-adjectives, so 綺麗じゃない, never 綺麗くない.

Examples

A friend picks up the new game you've been playing and asks if it's easy.

簡単じゃないよ。

"It's not easy."

簡単 (easy) + じゃない.

Casual

A coworker asks if you can help out tonight.

すみません、今日は暇じゃないです。

"Sorry, I'm not free today."

Polite

A friend offers you natto.

ごめん、納豆は好きじゃない。

"Sorry, I don't like natto."

好き is a な-adjective too, so 好きじゃない.

Casual

The hotel staff asks how your room is.

あまり静かじゃありません。

"It's not very quiet."

じゃありません is the stiffer polite one. Same meaning as じゃないです.

Polite

With and without

Is

静かだ。

"It's quiet."

Isn't

静かじゃない。

"It's not quiet." Just add じゃない.

Polite

静かじゃないです。

Same thing, polite. Also fine: 静かじゃありません.

Not this

静かくない。

くない is for い-adjectives (高い → 高くない). な-adjectives use じゃない.

好き + じゃない: doesn't like. あまり makes it "not really".

現実的 (realistic) is a な-adjective. まったく is "not at all", like 全然.

"I don't like sweet things."

好き is a な-adjective: 好きじゃない. んです makes it polite and explains.

"I don't like cases like this."

好き ("like") + じゃない = "don't like". こういう事件: "cases like this".

Casual

"I don't like that kind of thinking."

好き ("like") + じゃない = "don't like". そういう考え: "that kind of thinking".

Polite

お父さんは お好きじゃないですか？

"Doesn't your father like it?"

お好き (polite 好き) + じゃないです + か = "doesn't he like it?". A polite negative question.

N5 Grammar

な-Adjective (Past)

Polite綺麗でした
Casual綺麗だった

Same meaning: "it was beautiful". Only the politeness changes.

YouTube · video

想像以上に綺麗でした。

"It was even more beautiful than I imagined."

To say how something was with a な-adjective, add だった right after it, no な: 綺麗 → 綺麗だった. It works exactly like a noun: 学生だった.

On this card, the speaker just saw the place. The sentence answers "How was it?": beautiful, more than expected. 想像以上に is "beyond what I imagined".

Polite: でした, like on this card: 綺麗でした. Watch out: 綺麗 ends in い but is a な-adjective, so never 綺麗かった.

Examples

A friend asks how the new hotel was.

すごく静かだったよ。

"It was really quiet."

Casual

A coworker asks about your move.

大変でした。

"It was tough."

Polite

Your friend asks if you still play the piano.

子どもの頃は好きだったけど…。

"I liked it as a kid, but…"

好き is a な-adjective too, so 好きだった.

Casual

Someone asks how the hotel location was.

駅の前で、便利でした。

"It was right by the station, so it was handy."

Polite

With and without

Now

元気だ。

"I'm fine." Right now.

Was

元気だった。

"I was fine." Just add だった.

Polite

元気でした。

Same thing, polite.

Not this

綺麗かった。

かった is for い-adjectives (高い → 高かった). 綺麗 only looks like one.

必要 (needed) is a な-adjective: 必要でした, "was needed".

"The moonlight was really beautiful last night."

きれい + でした. とても is "very".

"I liked the one with blond hair."

"That must have been rough."

大変 ("tough, rough") + だった = "it was tough". ね: sharing the feeling, "that must have been rough".

ずっと 幸せだったよ。

"I was always happy."

幸せ ("happy") + だった = "was happy". ずっと: "the whole time". よ: telling them plainly.

Casual

心配 ("worried") + だった = "was worried". だから: "that's why".

N5 Grammar

好き・嫌い

Polite

YouTube · video

私はあんパンが好きです。

"I like anpan."

好き means "liked". It's not a verb, it's a な-adjective that describes the thing: "anpan is liked (by me)". So the thing you like gets が, not を.

On this card, she answers "What do you like?": 私は (as for me) + あんパン + が + 好きです.

好きです is polite, 好き or 好きだ is casual. Before a noun it takes な: 好きな食べ物, "favorite food".

Polite

YouTube · video

じゃあ、名古屋の嫌いなところは何ですか?

"So what do you dislike about Nagoya?"

嫌い is the opposite, "disliked", and works exactly like 好き: が before it, な before a noun (嫌いなところ). It ends in い but it's a な-adjective, so never 嫌くない.

嫌い is strong, close to "hate". To say "I don't really like it", people usually say あまり好きじゃない.

Examples

A new coworker asks what you do on weekends.

山が好きです。よく登ります。

"I like mountains. I climb a lot."

The thing you like + が + 好きです.

Polite

A friend offers you natto at breakfast.

ごめん、納豆嫌い。

"Sorry, I hate natto."

Casual: plain 嫌い, and the が drops out.

Casual

Your host asks if you eat spicy food.

辛いものはあまり好きじゃないです。

"I don't really like spicy food."

The soft way to say you dislike something. は instead of が, because you're contrasting it with other food.

Polite

Two friends scrolling through a music app.

好きなバンドある？

"Got a favorite band?"

好き + な + noun: "a band you like", which is how Japanese says "favorite".

Casual

With and without

Without

猫です。

"It's a cat." You're just naming it.

With 好き

猫が好きです。

"I like cats." Now it's about how you feel about it.

Without

食べ物は何ですか？

"What's the food?" Just asking which food it is.

With 嫌いな

嫌いな食べ物は何ですか？

"What food do you dislike?" 嫌い + な describes the food.

Add か to ask "do you like...?". は instead of が because fast food is the topic she's bringing up.

Polite

"I love nature like this."

大好き: "really like, love". Works the same way.

Casual

馬刺しが好き。

"I like horse sashimi."

馬刺し ("horse sashimi") + が + 好き = "I like horse sashimi". Casual: no です.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 11

俺は　サウナが好きなんだ。

"I like saunas."

サウナ ("sauna") + が + 好き + なんだ = "I like saunas, you see". なんだ explains something about himself.

Casual

YouTube · video

リアリティ番組が、あまり好きじゃないん。

"I'm not very fond of reality shows."

The soft "dislike": あまり好きじゃない instead of 嫌い.

Polite

Weakest Beast · Episode 7

"I do like it."

好き ("like") + ですよ = "I do like it". よ: telling them plainly, in case they doubted it.

N5 Grammar

上手・下手

Examples

Your friend sings at karaoke and nails it.

歌が上手だね！

"You're good at singing!"

The thing someone is good at + が + 上手. Same as 好き: が, not を.

Casual

A coworker asks if you cook at home.

いえ、料理が下手なんです。

"No, I'm bad at cooking."

下手 about yourself is fine. It sounds modest.

Polite

You watch a kid at the pool.

泳ぐのが上手ですね。

"He's good at swimming."

With a verb, add の first: 泳ぐ + の + が. The の turns the action into a noun, because が can't come right after a verb. 泳ぐが上手 is wrong.

Polite

Your friend can't fix their bike.

もっと上手な人に聞いて。

"Ask someone who's better at it."

上手 and 下手 are な-adjectives, so before a noun they take な: 上手な人, a skilled person.

Casual

At a job interview: "What are you good at?"

料理が得意です。

"Cooking is my strong point."

Don't say 上手 about yourself, it sounds like bragging. Say 得意 (my strong point) instead. The opposite is 苦手 (my weak point, "not my thing"). Both work like 上手: が before, な before a noun.

Polite

With and without

Without

歌が好きだね。

"You like singing." Says nothing about how well.

With 上手

歌が上手だね。

"You're good at singing." Now it's about skill.

Without

毎日泳ぎます。

"I swim every day." Just what you do.

With のが下手

泳ぐのが下手です。

"I'm bad at swimming." Verb + の + が + 下手.

Casual

Source unknown No source

考えてはいるけど伝えられない？そう、何か話すの下手なの。

"You think it, but can't say it? Yeah, I'm just bad at talking."

Verb + の + 下手. In casual speech the が often drops out.

Polite

Source unknown No source

全日本の女子バレーボールチームは、上手です。

"Japan's women's volleyball team is good."

No が here: what they're good at is obvious, so just 上手です.

Polite

Source unknown No source

祖父は、木工品を作るのが得意です。

"My grandpa is great at making things out of wood."

得意 works like 上手: verb + の + が + 得意.

Casual

Source unknown No source

下手なマッサージより、スパにいきたいよ。

"I'd rather go to a spa than get a bad massage."

下手 + な + noun: a massage done badly.

Polite

Fairy Tail · Episode 152

はい、とっても上手です。

"Yes, you're really good!"

上手です: you're good at it. Said about someone else, never yourself.

Casual

I am Mita, Your Housekeeper · Episode 9

三田 料理とっても上手なんだよ。

"Mita's really good at cooking!"

Skill + 上手: 料理(が)上手, good at cooking.

Casual

Overprotected Kahoko · Episode 10

ごめんね、下手な演奏で。

"Sorry it was so bad."

下手 is a な-adjective, so before a noun it takes な: 下手な演奏, a clumsy performance.

"And he's pretty good at cooking, too..."

料理も上手: good at cooking too.

N5 Grammar

～くなる・～になる

Polite

YouTube · video

でも、大人になって、温泉が好きになりました。

"But once I grew up, I came to like hot springs." [as a kid I didn't]

なる means to become: something changes from one state to another. After a noun or a な-adjective, add に: 大人になる = "become an adult", 好きになる = "come to like".

On this card, it answers "what changed?": before, he wasn't an adult and didn't like onsen. Now both are true.

Polite: なります / なりました. Casual: なる / なった.

Polite

YouTube · video

え、お家をちょっと、え、改築して大きくなりました。

"Um, we remodeled the house a bit, and it got bigger."

With an い-adjective, swap the last い for く: 大きい → 大きくなる = "get bigger". No に here.

Examples

You step outside in November.

寒くなったね。

"It's gotten cold, huh."

寒い ("cold") → 寒く + なった ("became") = "it's gotten cold". The い turns into く before なる.

Casual

A kid asks what you wanted to be when you were little.

医者になりたかったです。

"I wanted to become a doctor."

医者 is a noun, so it's 医者になる.

Polite

Your friend's Japanese has improved a lot.

日本語、上手になったね！

"Your Japanese got really good!"

上手 is a な-adjective, so it takes に too: 上手になる.

Casual

You look at the clock while gaming.

え、もう十時になった！

"Wait, it's already ten?!"

Times "become" too: it turned ten o'clock.

Casual

You look at the price tag again after a year.

高くなりましたね。

"It's gotten more expensive."

高い → 高く. The い always turns into く before なる.

Polite

With and without

Without

部屋が暗い。

"The room is dark." Just how it is right now.

With なる

部屋が暗くなった。

"The room got dark." It was bright before, and something changed: the sun went down, the light went off.

Polite

YouTube · video

とても緊張して、頭が真っ白になりました。

"I was so nervous my mind went blank."

Literally "my head became pure white". 真っ白 is a な-adjective, so に.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 5

すれ違いになったら大変。

"It'd be a pain if we ended up missing each other."

すれ違い (missing each other) is a noun, so に. なったら = "if it becomes".

Polite

YouTube · video

これは迷子になりますよ。

"You could totally get lost here."

迷子 means "lost child", so 迷子になる is "become lost". The everyday way to say "get lost".

Casual

ケンカになって

"...and it turned into a fight."

ケンカ ("a fight") + に + なって ("became, and...") = "it turned into a fight". Nouns take に before なる.

Casual

素直になったら？

"Why don't you just be honest?"

素直 ("honest, open") + に + なったら ("if you became") = "why don't you just be honest?".

Polite

友達、誰も来てくれなくなりますよ。

"None of our friends will come anymore."

ない → なくなる: it gets to the point where nobody comes.

Polite

Hyouka · Episode 17

"Sorry it's late, but I brought it."

遅い → 遅くなる: became late.

N5 Grammar

～く・～に (Adverbs)

YouTube · video

バッテリーが、今本当に早くなくなります。

"The battery runs out really fast now."

く turns an い-adjective into a word that describes the action: 早い (fast) → 早く (fast, quickly). Drop the い, add く.

On this card, it answers "How does it run out?": fast. 本当に (really) is the same trick on a noun: 本当 + に.

な-adjectives take に instead: 静か → 静かに (quietly). Politeness comes from the verb at the end, here なくなります.

YouTube · video

へえ。もうなんか、普通にスーパーで、適当にいつも買ってた。

"Huh. I always just grabbed them at the supermarket without thinking."

The な-adjective version, with に: 適当 (random, whatever) → 適当に (without much thought). 普通 (normal) → 普通に (just, normally).

Examples

Your friend is walking way too slowly.

早く来て！

"Come on, hurry!"

早い ("early, fast") → 早く = "quickly". 来て: "come!".

Casual

A sign in a library.

静かにしてください。

"Please be quiet."

静か ("quiet") → 静かに = "quietly". 静かにする: "be quiet".

Polite

A kid shows you their drawing.

上手に描けたね。

"You drew that really well."

上手 ("skillful") → 上手に = "well". 描けた: "could draw".

Casual

At the hairdresser.

髪を短く切ってください。

"Please cut my hair short."

短い ("short") → 短く = "short", saying how to cut it.

Polite

Someone asks how you slept.

昨日はよく寝た。

"I slept well last night."

いい ("good") → よく = "well". いい is the odd one: its く form comes from 良い.

Casual

With and without

Without

静かな部屋です。

"It's a quiet room." 静かな describes the room, a noun.

With に

静かに話してください。

"Please talk quietly." 静かに describes how you talk.

"In Uji you can easily find really quiet places like this."

簡単 (easy) → 簡単に (easily). Before a noun it stays 静かな.

"Go, quickly!"

早い becomes 早く to say how to go.

Casual

Source unknown No source

炭治郎みたいに、速く歩けないでしょう？

"You can't walk as fast as Tanjiro, right?"

速い ("fast") → 速く = "fast". 歩けない: "can't walk".

きれい is a な-adjective, so it takes に: きれいにする, "make it clean".

静か + に + なる: "became quiet".

N5 Grammar

より・～の方が

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 6

まっ、コーヒーより、ウイスキーのほうが多かったかもな。

"Well, maybe there was more whiskey in it than coffee."

より means than, and の方が marks the one that's more: ウイスキーの方が多い = the whiskey is more.

Put より right after the thing you compare against: コーヒーより (than coffee). On this card, the sentence answers "Which was more?": the whiskey.

Each half works alone too: コーヒーより多い, or ウイスキーの方が多い. 方 is often written ほう. Politeness comes from the end: 多かったです.

Examples

Choosing a drink with a friend.

コーヒーより紅茶の方が好き。

"I like tea more than coffee."

Casual

Comparing cities with a coworker.

東京は大阪より大きいです。

"Tokyo is bigger than Osaka."

Only より here: Tokyo is already the topic.

Polite

A friend asks: bus or train?

電車の方が早いよ。

"The train's faster."

Only の方が: the other one is clear.

Casual

Holding two bags in a shop.

どちらの方が軽いですか。

"Which one is lighter?"

どちらの方が...? = which one is more...?

Polite

With and without

Without

ウイスキーが多い。

"There's a lot of whiskey." No comparison.

With より・の方が

コーヒーよりウイスキーの方が多い。

"There's more whiskey than coffee." Now it's a comparison.

After an adjective it's just 方が, no の.

Daily Lives of High School Boys · Episode 6

あの人は俺よりバカなんだよ。

"She's dumber than me."

俺 ("me") + より + バカ ("stupid") = "dumber than me". なんだよ: explaining, a bit fed up.

N5 Grammar

一番 (いちばん)

Comprehensible Japanese · これ、それ、あれ、どれ

これが一番大きい松ぼっくりです。

"This is the biggest pine cone."

一番 means "number one". Put it right before an adjective and it means the most: 一番 + 大きい = "the biggest".

On this card, out of all the pine cones, this one wins. The sentence answers "Which one is the biggest?": これ.

一番 is the same in polite and casual speech. The politeness comes from the end: です here, だ or nothing with friends.

Examples

Showing a friend a family photo.

家族の中で、父が一番背が高いです。

"In my family, my dad is the tallest."

X の中で = "among X". It sets the group, then 一番 picks the winner.

Polite

A friend asks about the seasons in Japan.

秋が一番好きです。

"I like autumn the most."

一番好き = "favorite". Very common.

Polite

Looking at three cakes in a bakery window.

どれが一番おいしい？

"Which one is the tastiest?"

Question word + が + 一番. Use どれ for three or more things.

Casual

A kid asks about mountains.

日本で一番高い山は富士山だよ。

"The tallest mountain in Japan is Mt. Fuji."

Place + で sets the area: "in Japan".

Casual

With and without

Without

この部屋は広いです。

"This room is big." Just a description, no comparison.

With 一番

この部屋が一番広いです。

"This room is the biggest." Now it beats all the other rooms.

Notice は turns into が. With 一番 you're picking one thing out of a group, and が is the particle for "this one, not the others".

N5 Grammar

とても

YouTube · video

色付けが、とても綺麗ですね。

"The colours are really beautiful."

とても means very. It goes right before the describing word: とても + 綺麗 = "very beautiful".

On this card, it answers "how beautiful?" with "a lot". Without it, 綺麗ですね is just "it's beautiful".

とても itself never changes. Polite or casual only shows at the end: とても綺麗ですね / とても綺麗だね.

Examples

Small talk with a neighbour on a winter morning.

今日はとても寒いですね。

"It's very cold today, isn't it."

Polite

Someone asks what your hometown is like.

とても静かな町です。

"It's a very quiet town."

Before a noun, とても still sits in front of the describing word: とても静かな + 町.

Polite

You get home after a long day of moving boxes.

とても疲れた。

"I'm really tired."

とても also works with feeling words that are verbs: 疲れる, 困る, 驚く.

Casual

A friend lets you try their curry.

とってもおいしい！

"Super tasty!"

とても sounds a little neat. With friends, people often say とっても (warmer, stronger) or すごく instead.

Casual

With and without

Without

この本は面白いです。

"This book is interesting." A plain fact.

With とても

この本はとても面白いです。

"This book is very interesting." You really mean it.

N5 Grammar

ちょっと

YouTube · video

これちょっと日本の墨絵みたいですね。

"This looks a bit like Japanese ink painting."

ちょっと means a little, a bit. It goes right before the part it makes smaller: ちょっと + 墨絵みたい = "a bit like ink painting".

On this card, the sentence answers "Does it look like ink painting?": a bit, not completely. Without ちょっと it would just be "it looks like ink painting".

Japanese also use ちょっと to soften things: ちょっと待って (wait a sec), or 今日はちょっと… to say no gently. ちょっと never changes; polite or casual only shows at the end.

Examples

You try on a jacket in a shop. Your friend asks how it fits.

ちょっと大きい。

"It's a bit big."

Casual

At a restaurant, the waiter asks how the curry is.

ちょっと辛いです。

"It's a little spicy."

Polite

Your friend is about to leave, but you still need your shoes on.

ちょっと待って！

"Wait a sec!"

Here ちょっと isn't really "a little". It just makes 待って softer.

Casual

A coworker asks if you want to go drinking tonight. You don't.

今日はちょっと…。

"Today's a bit…"

The rest is left unsaid. Everyone understands it as a soft no.

Polite

With and without

Plain

この靴は大きい。

"These shoes are big."

With ちょっと

この靴はちょっと大きい。

"These shoes are a bit big."

Plain

待って！

"Wait!" Short and sharp.

With ちょっと

ちょっと待って！

"Wait a sec!" Same request, softer.

N5 Grammar

あまり～ない

YouTube · video

でも日本は地理的な条件で、あまりバナナを作っていません。

"But because of its geography, Japan doesn't grow many bananas."

あまり + a negative means not very, not much. あまり goes before the part it's about, and the sentence has to end negative: 作っていません, not 作っています.

On this card, the sentence answers "Does Japan grow bananas?": some, but not many. Without あまり it would be "Japan doesn't grow bananas" at all.

あまり itself never changes. Polite or casual shows at the end: あまり作っていません / あまり作ってない. In speech it's often あんまり.

Examples

A friend asks if the movie was good.

あまり面白くない。

"It's not that interesting."

面白い → 面白くない. あまり needs that ない.

Casual

A coworker asks if you drink.

あまり飲みません。

"I don't drink much."

Polite

Your friend asks if you're hungry.

あんまりお腹空いてない。

"I'm not that hungry."

あんまり is the spoken way to say あまり.

Casual

The teacher asks if you understood the explanation.

"I didn't really understand."

Polite

Plain

With あまり

"This cake isn't very sweet." A little, not much.

Polite

Same meaning, polite.

Not this

あまり needs a negative at the end. Without it the sentence breaks.

N5 Grammar

全然～ない

YouTube · video

とにかく最初は漫画の作り方も全然知らなくって

"Anyway, at first I didn't know anything about how to make manga either."

全然 (ぜんぜん) + a negative means not at all. It goes before the part it's about, and the sentence ends negative: 知らない, not 知る.

On this card, the sentence answers "Did you know how manga is made?": no, nothing. It's the strong version of あまり: あまり知らない is "don't know much", 全然知らない is "don't know at all".

全然 never changes. Polite or casual shows at the end: 全然知りません / 全然知らない. In everyday talk you'll also hear 全然大丈夫 ("totally fine"): no negative, but it still answers a worry with "not at all".

Examples

A friend asks if you slept well before the exam.

全然寝てない。

"I didn't sleep at all."

Casual

全然話せません。

"I can't speak it at all."

Polite

Your friend shows you a math problem.

全然分からない。

"I have no idea."

Casual

A coworker apologizes for being five minutes late.

全然大丈夫ですよ。

"It's totally fine."

The everyday 全然: no negative, but it answers "Is it a problem?" with "not at all".

"I don't really understand." A little, not much.

With 全然

"I don't understand at all." Nothing.

Same meaning, polite.

Not this

全然 needs a negative (or 大丈夫). Without it the sentence breaks.

ここに、お湯を入れます。

"[You] pour hot water in here."

ます goes on the end of a verb and makes it polite. 入れる (to put in) becomes 入れます. The meaning stays the same.

On this card, someone shows how to use something, step by step. The sentence answers "What do I do?".

Past: 入れました (put in). Not: 入れません (don't put in).

Examples

A coworker asks what you're doing this weekend.

京都に行きます。

"I'm going to Kyoto."

行く becomes 行き + ます. The last sound changes from u to i before ます.

Polite

The waiter asks if you liked the curry. The plate is empty.

全部食べました。

"I ate it all."

ました is the past of ます: 食べます (eat) → 食べました (ate).

Polite

Your host offers you a beer. You're driving.

お酒は飲みません。

"I don't drink alcohol."

ません is the "not" of ます: 飲みます (drink) → 飲みません (don't drink).

Polite

A client asks when you'll get to the office tomorrow.

9時に来ます。

"I'll come at 9."

来る → 来ます, read きます. ます covers "will" too: no separate future form.

Polite

With and without

Without ます

毎朝コーヒーを飲む。

"I drink coffee every morning." The verb as it is in the dictionary.

With ます

毎朝コーヒーを飲みます。

Same meaning, now polite. For people you don't know well, at work, in shops.

ru-verbs

食べる → 食べます

Ends in える or いる: take off る, add ます. 見る → 見ます.

u-verbs

飲む → 飲みます

The last u sound turns into i, then ます. 待つ → 待ちます, 帰る → 帰ります.

The two odd ones

する → します　来る → 来ます

来ます is read きます.

厳選する is "to choose carefully". する becomes します. ます also covers the future: "I'll do it".

ました is the past: 食べます → 食べました.

ある (there is) → あります → ありません (there isn't). 異常 is "something abnormal".

来る → 来ます → 来ました (came). Read きました.

完了する (to be completed) → 完了します → 完了しました.

始める → 始めます. る drops, ます goes on.

じゃまする ("to get in the way") + ます. A set phrase when you walk into someone's place.

N5 Grammar

る-Verb (Dictionary)

Polite食べます
Casual食べる

Same meaning: "to eat". Only the politeness changes.

る-verbs are the second big group of Japanese verbs. Their dictionary form always ends in る, and the sound right before it is an i or an e sound: 見る (miru), 食べる (taberu).

In Japanese they're called 一段 (ichidan), "one step": the front of the verb never changes. To use one, drop the る and add the ending: 食べ + ます, 食べ + ない, 食べ + た.

Watch out: a few verbs look like this but are う-verbs: 帰る, 入る, 走る, 知る. Those you just have to learn.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 20

モダン焼、できる？

"Can you make modan-yaki?"

できる is the dictionary form of a る-verb: the verb exactly as the dictionary lists it, ending in る. Said like this, it's casual.

On this card, it answers "Is that possible?". As a casual question, you just raise your voice at the end, no か needed.

Polite: drop the る and add ます: できます. Nothing else moves, and that's what makes it a る-verb.

Polite

YouTube · video

これは、すごく共感できます。

"I can really relate to this."

Same verb, polite: できる → できます. 共感できる = "can relate".

Examples

A friend asks about your Sunday mornings.

日曜日は、昼まで寝るよ。

"On Sundays I sleep till noon."

寝る (to sleep). Polite: 寝ます.

Casual

Asking a coworker about lunch.

いつもここで昼ご飯を食べますか。

"Do you always eat lunch here?"

食べる → 食べます.

Polite

Your friend asks what you're doing tonight.

今夜は家で映画を見る。

"I'm watching a movie at home tonight."

The dictionary form also works for the future.

Casual

Telling your teacher about your mornings.

毎朝六時に起きます。

"I get up at six every morning."

起きる → 起きます.

Polite

With and without

Without

パンを食べます。

"I eat bread." Polite, to a teacher or someone you don't know well.

With 食べる

パンを食べる。

"I eat bread." Same meaning, casual, to a friend.

N5 Grammar

う-Verb (Dictionary)

Polite行きます
Casual行く

Same meaning: "to go". Only the politeness changes.

う-verbs are the biggest group of Japanese verbs. Their dictionary form ends in an u sound: う, く, ぐ, す, つ, ぬ, ぶ, む or る. Watch out with る: many verbs ending in る are う-verbs (作る, 帰る), but not all (食べる isn't).

In Japanese they're called 五段 (godan), "five steps". When you change the verb, its last sound can move to any of the five sounds in its row of the kana chart: く can become か, き, け or こ. 書く → 書きます is one of those moves.

Casual

YouTube · video

例えば交流会に行く。

"For example, [you could] go to a meetup."

行く is the dictionary form: the verb exactly as the dictionary lists it, ending in an u sound (here く). Said like this, it's casual.

On this card, he's giving ideas for meeting people. The sentence answers "What could I do?": go to a meetup.

Polite: 行きます. The last sound moves from u to i (く → き), then ます goes on. That change is what makes it a う-verb.

Polite

YouTube · video

最近はあの岐阜県によく行きます。

"These days I often go to Gifu."

Same verb, polite: 行く → 行きます. You'd say it to people you don't know well.

Examples

Your friend asks if you're coming to karaoke tonight.

うん、行く！

"Yeah, I'm going!"

To a coworker: 行きます.

Casual

The barista asks if your coffee is to go.

ここで飲みます。

"I'll drink it here."

飲む → 飲みます: む becomes み.

Polite

Your friend texts: "running 10 minutes late, sorry!"

じゃあ、カフェで待つ。

"Okay, I'll wait at the café."

Polite: 待ちます. つ becomes ち.

Casual

A client asks when you'll send the finished drawings.

明日送ります。

"I'll send them tomorrow."

送る ends in る, but it's still a う-verb: る becomes り.

Polite

With and without

Dictionary form

毎日絵を描く。

"I draw every day." To a friend, or in your diary.

With ます

毎日絵を描きます。

Same meaning. To a client, a coworker, someone you just met.

Dictionary form

そろそろ帰る。

"I'm heading home soon." To friends at the party.

With ます

そろそろ帰ります。

Same thing, to your boss at the work dinner.

Every ending

Just to look things up. The last sound moves from the u row to the i row, then ます.

Dictionary→ます
買う→買いますbuy
書く→書きますwrite
急ぐ→急ぎますhurry
貸す→貸しますlend
待つ→待ちますwait
死ぬ→死にますdie
遊ぶ→遊びますplay
読む→読みますread
作る→作りますmake

Careful with る. 作る is a う-verb, so 作ります. But 食べる is a る-verb: る just drops, 食べます. Telling them apart gets its own page.

N5 Grammar

る-Verb (Negative)

Polite足りません
Casual足りない

Same meaning: "isn't enough". Only the politeness changes.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 2

少し塩気が足りないね

"[It] needs a little more salt."

To say a る-verb is not happening, drop the る and add ない: 足りる (to be enough) → 足りない (isn't enough).

On this card, he's tasting the food. The sentence answers "Is there enough salt?": no, it's a little short. The ね at the end is just "huh", sharing the thought.

Polite: drop the る and add ません: 足りません.

Polite

YouTube · video

あれ？！思ったほど散歩している人がいません。

"Huh?! There aren't as many people out walking as I thought."

Same move, polite: いる (to be there, for people and animals) → いません. Casual would be いない.

Examples

A friend holds out a pack of natto for you.

納豆は食べない。

"I don't eat natto."

To a coworker: 食べません.

Casual

A coworker asks if you saw the match last night.

サッカーはあまり見ません。

"I don't really watch soccer."

見る → 見ません. Just the る goes.

Polite

Your friend asks if you want to go out tonight. It's raining.

今日は出かけない。

"I'm not going out today."

ない works for "don't" and "won't". There's no separate future.

Casual

Your host family drops you at the airport on your last day.

この夏は忘れません。

"I won't forget this summer."

Polite

With and without

Plain

肉を食べる。

"I eat meat."

With ない

肉を食べない。

"I don't eat meat." る out, ない in.

Polite

肉を食べません。

Same meaning. る out, ません in.

Not this

肉を食べらない。

That's the う-verb move (帰る → 帰らない). る-verbs just drop the る.

N5 Grammar

う-Verb (Negative)

Polite分かりません
Casual分からない

Same meaning: "don't know". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

YouTube · video

"But this is a story about the gods, so we don't know if it's true."

To say a う-verb is not happening, politely: move the last sound from u to i, then add ません. 分かる (to know) → 分かりません. Same i sound as before ます.

On this card, the speaker is telling an old legend. The sentence answers "Is it true?": nobody knows.

Casual

You and a coworker look out the window. It's been raining all day.

雨がなかなか止みません。

"The rain just won't stop."

ません works for "don't" and "won't". There's no separate future.

Polite

Plain

With ない

コーヒーを飲まない。

"I don't drink coffee." む → ま, then ない.

Polite

コーヒーを飲みません。

Same meaning. む → み, then ません.

Not this

ない never goes straight on the dictionary form. The last sound has to change first.

Polite食べました
Casual食べた

Polite行きました

Plain

With た

ある (to be there, for things) → ありました. Casual: あった.

Casual

New Atashin'chi · Episode 1

分かったからシーッ！

"Okay, I get it, so shh!"

分かる (to understand) → 分かった. It ends in る, so った.

Casual

YouTube · video

子どもの頃、僕が山で遊んだ時、毎日冒険みたいな感じでした。

"When I played in the mountains as a kid, every day felt like an adventure."

遊ぶ (to play) → 遊んだ. ぶ goes to んだ. Before 時 (when) the casual form stays, even in a polite sentence.

Casual

Source unknown No source

先週、彼と会議室で話した。

"I talked with him in the meeting room last week."

話す (to talk) → 話した. す goes to した.

Casual

Source unknown No source

"I put the magnifying glass on the desk."

置く (to put) → 置いた. く goes to いた.

N5 Grammar

Verb (Past negative)

Polite行きませんでした standard polite
行かなかったです everyday, softer
Casual行かなかった

Same meaning: "didn't go". Only the politeness changes.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 12

常勤パンダさんが、モデラーなんて知らなかったよ。

"I didn't know Full-Time Panda built models."

なかった means didn't: the negative, in the past. Take the ない form and swap ない for なかった: 知らない → 知らなかった.

On this card, it answers "Did you know?": no, not until now. It works the same for every verb: 食べない → 食べなかった, しない → しなかった, 来ない → 来なかった.

Polite: swap ます for ませんでした: 知ります → 知りませんでした.

Polite

NHK News Web Easy · article

前半は、日本もオランダも点が取れませんでした。

"In the first half, neither Japan nor the Netherlands scored."

Polite: 取れます → 取れませんでした. 取れる = "can get", so literally "couldn't get a point".

Examples

A friend asks how the party was.

昨日、パーティーに行かなかった。

"I didn't go to the party yesterday."

行かない → 行かなかった.

Casual

Your teacher asks for your homework.

すみません、宿題をしませんでした。

"Sorry, I didn't do my homework."

します → しませんでした.

Polite

A coworker offers you a snack.

今朝は何も食べませんでした。

"I didn't eat anything this morning."

何も + negative = nothing.

Polite

A friend asks if you saw their message.

ごめん、見なかった。

"Sorry, I didn't see it."

見ない → 見なかった.

Casual

With and without

Without

パーティーに行かない。

"I'm not going to the party." Now or later.

With なかった

パーティーに行かなかった。

"I didn't go to the party." It's over, and I wasn't there.

Polite

YouTube · video

"My stomach didn't feel heavy."

なかった + です: polite, a bit softer than ませんでした.

Polite

YouTube · video

"I couldn't even say simple phrases like that."

話せる (can speak) → 話せませんでした.

ネットに繋がらなくて、開けませんでした。

"It wasn't online, so I couldn't open it."

開けます → 開けませんでした.

Polite

Source unknown No source

階段の上には、誰もいませんでした。

"There was nobody at the top of the stairs."

いる → いませんでした. 誰も + negative = nobody.

Casual

Source unknown No source

あれ？ウケなかった？

ウケる (to get a laugh) → ウケなかった.

Casual

Source unknown No source

"I had a nightmare last night and couldn't sleep well."

眠れる (can sleep) → 眠れなかった.

Casual

"I had no idea."

知る ("know") → 知らない → 知らなかった = "didn't know", "I had no idea".

Casual

できる ("can do") → できない → できなかった = "couldn't do". なんにも (spoken 何も): "anything".

N5 Grammar

来る

Polite来ます (きます)
Casual来る (くる)

Same meaning: "to come". Only the politeness changes.

Casual

YouTube · video

ここには、ゴンドラで来ることもできる。

"You can also come here by gondola."

来る (くる) means to come: to move toward the place where the speaker is, or will be. It's an irregular verb, so the kanji stays the same but the reading changes (くる, き, こ).

On this card, the sentence answers "How can you get here?": by gondola. 来る is the casual dictionary form, and it sits right before こと.

Polite

YouTube · video

はい、今、注文した五平餅が来ました！見えますか？

"Okay, the gohei-mochi I ordered just arrived! Can you see it?"

Polite past: 来る → 来ました (きました). The food came to the table where he is, so 来る is "arrived". Casual would be 来た (きた).

Examples

You're on the phone with a friend. Your dinner plans are tonight.

今夜、うちに来る？

"Are you coming to my place tonight?"

Just 来る with a rising voice, no か needed.

Casual

You're the manager. A new hire is starting tomorrow.

明日は何時に来ますか。

"What time will you come tomorrow?"

来る → 来ます. Say it きます.

Polite

A friend asks if Ken is joining the barbecue.

ケンは今日は来ないよ。

"Ken isn't coming today."

Not 来らない. The く turns into こ: こない. Polite: 来ません (きません).

Casual

Your friend asks who showed up at the office this morning.

社長が朝早く来ました。

"The boss came in early this morning."

Polite

Your mom calls you down: dinner is ready.

今、行く！

"I'm coming!"

English says "coming", Japanese says "going" (行く) when you head to where the other person is. 来る is for coming to where you are, or will be.

Casual

With and without

Casual

友達が来る。

"A friend comes." Reading: くる.

Not coming

友達が来ない。

"A friend doesn't come." Reading: こない.

Polite

友達が来ます。

Same as 来る, polite. Reading: きます.

Not this

友達が来らない。

That's the う-verb move (帰る → 帰らない). 来る is irregular: く becomes こ.

来て + います (said as 来てます). They came and they're still here, so English says "are here".

"I've been to this building, too."

来た (casual past) + ことがあります = "I have done it before".

"The sushi's here!"

来ました (きました): polite past.

また ("again") + 来る (くる) = "I'll come again". The dictionary form covers "will".

Casual

"Did someone come?"

誰か ("someone") + 来た (きた, "came") = "did someone come?". の makes it a soft question.

Casual

"What are you here for?!"

何しに ("to do what") + 来た ("came") = "what did you come here for?!". Rough and angry.

Casual

Million Yen Woman · Episode 1

"Where did you come from?"

どっから (spoken どこから, "from where") + 来た ("came") = "where did you come from?".

N5 Grammar

する

Politeします
Casualする

Same meaning: "to do". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

YouTube · video

皆さんは、１日の終わりに何をしますか？

"What do you all do at the end of the day?"

する means to do. The thing you do comes before it with を (何をする, テニスをする), or an action noun sits right in front of it (勉強する, 料理する).

It's an irregular verb: in most forms the す turns into し (します, しない, した). On this card, the sentence asks "What activity?": 何をしますか.

Casual

Pokémon The Series: Indigo League · Episode 2

悪役さん、わたしが相手をするわ。

"Hey, villain, I'll take you on."

Casual dictionary form する, here for something she's about to do. 相手をする is "be someone's opponent". The わ at the end just softens it.

Examples

You're texting a friend on Friday night.

週末、何する？

"What are you doing this weekend?"

In casual speech the を often drops out: 何をする → 何する.

Casual

A coworker asks what you do in the evenings.

毎晩、日本語の勉強をします。

"I study Japanese every evening."

勉強をします and 勉強します mean the same thing.

Polite

Your roommate asks if you're cleaning today. You're tired.

今日は掃除しない。

"I'm not cleaning today."

Not すらない. The す turns into し: しない. Polite: しません.

Casual

Your teacher asks what you did yesterday.

友達とテニスをしました。

"I played tennis with a friend."

English says "play", Japanese just says "do" for sports and games.

Polite

Your friend lent you a new game last week.

あのゲーム、もうした？

"Did you play that game yet?"

Casual past: する → した. Polite: しました.

Casual

With and without

Casual

宿題をする。

"I do homework."

Not doing

宿題をしない。

"I don't do homework."

Polite

宿題をします。

Same as する, polite.

Not this

宿題をすらない。

That's the う-verb move (帰る → 帰らない). する is irregular: す becomes し.

Polite

YouTube · video

見て、私はつけ麺を注文しましたよ。

"Look, I ordered tsukemen."

注文 (an order) + する = to order. Polite past: しました.

Polite

YouTube · video

最近、いつも僕は朝早い時間、赤ちゃんのお世話をします。

"These days I always look after the baby early in the morning."

お世話をする = to take care of. します for something he does every day.

"Excuse me."

失礼 ("rudeness") + します = "excuse me". Said when you walk into or out of a room.

Polite

しません。

"We won't."

する ("do") → しません = "we won't do it". A flat, polite refusal.

Casual

したよ…

"I did."

する ("do") → した = "I did". よ: telling them, a bit defensive.

Casual

"What should we have?"

何 ("what") + する ("do") = "what'll we do?", here "what should we order?". を dropped, casual.

Casual

"What's wrong?"

どう ("how") + した ("did") = "what happened?", the everyday "what's wrong?".

N5 Grammar

Verb + Noun

Casual

YouTube · video

今住んでいるところは千葉県。

"Where I live now is Chiba."

A verb can sit right before a noun to describe it. Here 住んでいる (live) + ところ (place) = the place where I live.

Just put the plain verb in front: no の, no な, nothing in between. On this card, it answers "Which place?": the one I live in now.

The verb before the noun stays plain even in polite speech: 住んでいるところです. Only the end of the sentence shows the politeness.

Polite

YouTube · video

2025年に、大ヒットした映画があります。

"There's a movie that was a huge hit in 2025."

Past works too: 大ヒットした (was a big hit) + 映画 = a movie that was a big hit. Polite only because of あります at the end.

Examples

At a party, pointing at someone.

あそこでビールを飲んでいる人は誰？

"Who's that guy drinking beer over there?"

Everything before 人 describes the person.

Casual

Telling a coworker about a book.

昨日買った本はとても面白いです。

"The book I bought yesterday is really good."

買った (bought) + 本 = the book I bought.

Polite

Looking at a menu with a friend.

食べたいもの、ある？

"Anything you want to eat?"

たい works too: 食べたい + もの = a thing I want to eat.

Casual

Asking a station worker.

新宿に行く電車はどれですか。

"Which train goes to Shinjuku?"

行く + 電車 = the train that goes.

Polite

With and without

Without

これは本です。

"This is a book." Just some book.

With Verb + Noun

これは昨日買った本です。

"This is the book I bought yesterday." The verb tells you which book.

Polite

食べられる (can eat) + もの = things you can eat.

来る + 人 = people who come.

揚げた (fried) + もの = the thing you fried.

"It was a fulfilling life."

充実した describes 人生: a life that was full.

"There are lots of places like this that sell electronics."

売っている (are selling) + 場所 = places that sell.

Casual

あ、夜、夜食べる人はもうサクっと食べて。

"Oh, if you're having it at night, just eat it quick."

食べる + 人 = people who eat.

あのね、ピカチュウ、この状態ずーっと続ける気？

"Hey, Pikachu, you plan to keep this up forever?"

続ける (to keep going) + 気 (intention) = the plan to keep going.

YouTube · video

"In spring there are sakura buns, and even ones with mochi inside."

入っている (is inside) + もの = ones that have it inside.

N5 Grammar

～に行く・～に来る

YouTube · video

意地悪なサルに、お返しをしに行きます。

"We're going to go get back at the mean monkey." [a folk tale]

～に行く means go to do something. It answers "going to do what?": here, to get back at the monkey.

Take the verb's ます-form, drop ます, add に行く: します → しに行く, 食べます → 食べに行く. Activity nouns work too: 買い物に行く, スキーに行く.

With 来る it's "come to do something": 遊びに来る. Polite: に行きます, に来ます. Casual: に行く, に来る.

Examples

You're heading out. You tell your roommate where you're going.

コンビニに飲み物を買いに行くね。

"I'm going to the convenience store to get drinks."

Two に: コンビニに = where, 買いに = to do what.

Casual

Monday at work. A coworker asks about your weekend.

海に泳ぎに行きました。

"I went to the beach for a swim."

泳ぎます → 泳ぎ + に行きました.

Polite

Your friend shows up at your door without warning.

え、何しに来たの？

"Huh, what are you here for?"

Literally "came to do what?". 何しに is a very common question.

Casual

At a party, someone asks why you came to Japan.

日本語を勉強しに来ました。

"I came to study Japanese."

You're in Japan now, so it's 来る, not 行く.

Polite

With and without

Without

図書館に行きます。

"I'm going to the library." Only where.

With ～に行く

図書館に本を返しに行きます。

"I'm going to the library to return a book." Where, and what for.

An activity noun works too: パターゴルフに行く, "go (to play) mini golf".

友達と、酎ハイを飲みに行きました。

"I went for chuhai with my friends."

飲む → 飲み + に行く: "go to drink". Going out for drinks.

Casual

Source unknown No source

ここに、カツ丼を食べに来るんだ。

"He comes here to eat katsudon." [his victory meal]

Same pattern with 来る: 食べ + に来る, "come (here) to eat".

Polite

Source unknown No source

昨日、叔母が家に遊びに来ました。

"Yesterday my aunt came over to visit."

遊びに来る: "come over, come to visit". Very common.

Casual

Source unknown No source

友達と一緒に、富士山を見に行った。

"I went to see Mount Fuji with a friend."

見る → 見 + に行く: "go to see".

Polite

Source unknown No source

母は、食料品を買いに行きました。

"My mom went to buy groceries."

買う → 買い + に行く: "go to buy".

Casual

Source unknown No source

一度、動物園に遊びに来てよ。

"Come visit the zoo sometime."

Two に: 動物園に = where, 遊びに = to do what.

N5 Grammar

～な (Don't)

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 11

串ごと食うなよ。

"Don't eat the skewer too." [the stick and all]

な after a verb means don't: a short, blunt order not to do something.

It goes straight after the dictionary form, nothing changes: 食う → 食うな, する → するな. On this card, it answers "what must I not do?": eat the stick.

It's rough, so you hear it between friends, from parents, on signs and in anime. The よ softens it a little. The polite way to say don't is ないでください.

Examples

Your friend is about to give up on the last kilometer of a run.

諦めるな！

"Don't give up!"

諦める ("give up") + な = "don't give up!". Dictionary form + な: a blunt "don't".

Your friend is nervous before a job interview.

心配するなよ。大丈夫だって。

"Don't worry. You'll be fine."

する → するな. The よ makes it friendlier.

You're about to tell everyone your friend's secret.

言うな！

"Don't say it!"

A kid runs along the edge of the pool. The lifeguard shouts.

走るな！

"No running!"

A sign next to a river.

ゴミを捨てるな

"Don't dump trash."

Signs use な because it's short and firm.

Watch out: not every な at the end is "don't". You step outside in winter.

今日は寒いな。

"Man, it's cold today."

After an adjective, な is just a feeling, like "huh" or "man". "Don't" only comes after a verb, said like an order.

With and without

Without

それ、食べる？

"Are you going to eat that?" Just asking.

With な

それ、食べるな！

"Don't eat that!" You're stopping them.

心配する ("worry") + な = "don't worry". Blunt, but here it's meant kindly.

気にする ("mind, worry about") + な = "don't worry about it".

勘違いする ("get the wrong idea") + な = "don't get the wrong idea".

来る ("come") + な = "don't come!". Shouted, so very blunt.

Casual

押し通る、邪魔するな！

"I'm coming through, don't get in my way!"

邪魔する ("get in the way") + な = "don't get in my way!". 押し通る: "I'm pushing through".

N5 Grammar

て-Form

YouTube · video

今日はめがねをはずして、コンタクトレンズをつけています。

"Today I took off my glasses and I'm wearing contacts."

The て-form is the verb shape that ends in て or で. On this card, はずす (take off) becomes はずして, and the sentence keeps going.

Make it like the past form, just swap た for て: はずした → はずして, 食べた → 食べて, 飲んだ → 飲んで. If you can say the past, you can say the て-form.

On its own it means "and" between actions. Lots of grammar sits on it: てください (please), ている (is doing), てから (after).

Examples

る-verbs: drop る, add て.

朝ご飯を食べて、学校に行きます。

"I eat breakfast and go to school."

食べる → 食べて. 見る → 見て, 寝る → 寝て.

Polite

Verbs ending in う, つ, る: っ + て.

ちょっと待って！

"Wait a sec!"

待つ → 待って. 買う → 買って, 帰る → 帰って.

Casual

Verbs ending in む, ぶ, ぬ: ん + で.

この薬を飲んでください。

"Please take this medicine."

飲む → 飲んで. 遊ぶ → 遊んで, 死ぬ → 死んで.

Polite

Verbs ending in く: い + て.

名前を書いてください。

"Please write your name."

書く → 書いて. One odd one: 行く → 行って.

Polite

Verbs ending in ぐ: い + で.

急いで！電車が来るよ。

"Hurry! The train's coming."

急ぐ → 急いで. 泳ぐ → 泳いで.

Casual

Verbs ending in す: し + て.

もっとゆっくり話してください。

"Please speak more slowly."

話す → 話して. 出す → 出して.

Polite

The two irregular ones.

明日、八時に来てください。

"Please come at eight tomorrow."

来る → 来て, する → して.

Polite

With and without

Without

本を読んだ。

"I read the book." Past, the sentence ends here.

With て

本を読んで、寝ました。

"I read the book and went to sleep." Same shape with で instead of だ, and it keeps going.

N5 Grammar

～て (And then)

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 2

朝起きて一番に、中庭に集まって、家族みんなで太極拳をします。

"First thing after we get up, we gather in the courtyard and the whole family does tai chi." [Panda talking about home]

て joins actions in the order they happen: get up, gather, do tai chi.

Put each verb in the て-form and keep going: 起きる → 起きて, 集まる → 集まって. Only the last verb shows the tense and the politeness, here します.

So you never need ます in the middle. To make it casual, change only the end: する instead of します.

Examples

Your friend asks about your evening.

家に帰って、シャワーを浴びて、寝ました。

"I went home, showered and went to bed."

Past only at the end: 寝ました. The て verbs are past too.

Polite

Telling a friend your plan for Sunday.

渋谷に行って、映画を見る。

"I'll go to Shibuya and watch a movie."

行く → 行って (the odd one).

Casual

Explaining the way to the station.

まっすぐ行って、二つ目の角を右に曲がってください。

"Go straight, then turn right at the second corner."

The last verb has てください, so the whole thing is a request.

Polite

Cooking with a friend.

玉ねぎを切って、炒めて。

"Cut the onion and fry it."

切る → 切って. 炒める → 炒めて.

Casual

With and without

Without

家に帰ります。ご飯を食べます。

"I go home. I eat." Two separate sentences.

With て

家に帰って、ご飯を食べます。

"I go home and eat." One sentence, one action after the other.

N5 Grammar

～くて・～で

YouTube · video

この辺は緑が多くて、きれいです。

"This area has lots of green, and it's pretty."

くて joins an い-adjective to what comes next, like "and": lots of green, and pretty.

Drop the last い and add くて: 多い → 多くて, 安い → 安くて. One odd one: いい → よくて.

For な-adjectives and nouns, use で instead: 静かで, 学生で. Only the end shows the politeness: です or nothing.

Examples

Your friend asks about the new ramen place.

安くて、おいしいよ。

"It's cheap and tasty."

安い → 安くて.

Casual

Describing your new apartment.

部屋は静かで、きれいです。

"The room is quiet and clean."

静か is a な-adjective, so で.

Polite

Introducing yourself.

私は学生で、二十歳です。

"I'm a student and I'm twenty."

学生 is a noun, so で.

Polite

Talking about a café.

雰囲気がよくて、よく行くんだ。

"The vibe is nice, so I go there a lot."

いい → よくて. Here it also gives the reason.

Casual

Without

このラーメンは安いです。おいしいです。

"This ramen is cheap. It's tasty." Two separate sentences.

With くて

このラーメンは安くて、おいしいです。

"This ramen is cheap and tasty." One smooth sentence.

N5 Grammar

～てください

Polite～てください
Casual～て

Same meaning: "please do". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

1 Litre of Tears · Episode 1

受験生は、急いでください。

"Exam takers, please hurry." [a staff member at the exam building]

てください after a verb means please do it: you ask someone to do something.

It goes on the て-form. Make it like the past form, just with て instead of た: 急いだ → 急いで, 食べた → 食べて, 行った → 行って. On this card, it answers "what do you want me to do?": hurry.

ください makes it polite: for strangers, shops, teachers. With friends you drop it and just say the て-form.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 14

大丈夫、任せて。

"It's fine, leave it to me."

Same request, just the て-form with nothing after it. 任せる → 任せて: "leave it (to me)".

Examples

In a shop, you point at a bag behind the counter.

そのかばんを見せてください。

"Please show me that bag."

見せる → 見せて.

Polite

You get into a taxi.

駅まで行ってください。

"To the station, please."

行く → 行って. Literally "please go to the station".

Polite

The teacher spoke too fast and you missed it.

もう一度言ってください。

"Could you say that again, please?"

言う → 言って.

Polite

Your friend is walking off and you still need your shoes on.

ちょっと待って！

"Wait a sec!"

待つ → 待って.

Casual

Your friend is busy right now.

じゃあ、あとで電話してね。

"Okay, call me later."

する → して. The ね makes it softer.

Casual

With and without

Without

窓を開けます。

"I'll open the window." You do it yourself.

With てください

窓を開けてください。

"Please open the window." You ask someone else to do it.

～ないでください

Same meaning: "please don't". Only the politeness changes.

ないでください after a verb means please don't: you ask someone not to do something.

It goes on the ない-form: 遊ぶ → 遊ばない → 遊ばないでください. If you can say "not", just add でください.

ください makes it polite: for strangers, customers, teachers. With friends you drop it and just say ないで.

N5 Grammar

～ている (Doing now)

Polite～ています
Casual～ている・～てる てる: spoken, everyday

Same meaning: "is doing". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

ている after a verb means it's going on right now: not "I drink", but "I'm drinking".

It goes on the て-form: 飲む → 飲んで → 飲んでいる. On this card, it answers "what are you doing?".

ています is polite. Casual is ている, and in speech the い usually drops: 飲んでる.

N5 Grammar

～ている (State)

Polite～ています
Casual～ている・～てる てる: spoken, everyday

Same meaning: a state that lasts. Only the politeness changes.

Polite

YouTube · video

今は岡崎に地元があるんですけど、今は名古屋に住んでいます。

"My hometown is Okazaki, but now I live in Nagoya."

With some verbs, ている isn't an action going on. It's a state that lasts: 住む is moving in, 住んでいる is living there now.

Same shape as "is doing": 住む → 住んで → 住んでいる. The common ones: 住んでいる (live), 持っている (have), 知っている (know), 結婚している (married), 着ている (wearing).

ています is polite. Casual is ている, and in speech the い usually drops: 住んでる.

Casual

"Oh no, oh no. They've got a machine gun." [playing a video game]

持つ is the moment you pick it up. 持ってる is having it now.

A coworker asks about your family.

姉は結婚しています。

"My older sister is married."

結婚する is the wedding day. 結婚している is being married.

Your friend mentions a café.

知る is finding out. 知っている is knowing.

着る is putting it on. 着ている is wearing it.

疲れる is getting tired. 疲れている is being tired.

N5 Grammar

～てから

YouTube · video

"I started getting up this early after my kid was born."

てから after a verb means after doing it: first one thing, then the rest.

It goes on the て-form: 生まれる → 生まれて + から. On this card, it answers "since when?" or "after what?": since the baby was born.

The politeness sits at the end of the sentence, not on てから. Plain ～て only says "and"; てから makes the order clear.

Examples

Your friend wants to go out right now.

"I'll go after I do my homework."

ほしい (欲しい)

Polite欲しいです
Casual欲しい

Same meaning: "want". Only the politeness changes.

N5 Grammar

～たい

Polite～たいです
Casual～たい

Same meaning: "want to". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

YouTube · video

今日は、ちょっと仮眠を取りたいですね。

"Today I'd like to grab a quick nap." [tired after traveling]

たい means want to: it's about an action you want to do, not a thing you want.

Take the ます form and swap ます for たい: 取ります → 取りたい. On this card, it answers "what do you feel like doing?": a nap.

Add です to make it polite: 取りたいです.

N5 Grammar

～ませんか

Polite行きませんか
Casual行かない？

Same meaning: "want to go?". Only the politeness changes.

ませんか is how you invite someone: "would you like to...?", "why don't we...?". Swap ます for ませんか: 行きます → 行きませんか.

Literally it's "won't you go?". Asking it the negative way is softer: it's easy for the other person to say no.

Casual: the ない form with a rising voice: 行かない？

Examples

Inviting a coworker.

一緒に昼ご飯を食べませんか。

"Would you like to have lunch together?"

食べます → 食べませんか.

Polite

Casual: the ない form, voice up at the end.

休む → 休まない.

N5 Grammar

でも (Or something)

Pokémon The Series: Indigo League · Episode 2

何とかするよ弁償でも何でも。

"I'll sort it out. Pay you back [for the bike] or whatever."

でも goes right after a noun and means "or something". It takes the place of を or が.

On this card, the noun becomes just an example: paying back is one idea, but he'll do anything. 何でも adds "or anything at all".

Same in polite and casual speech. You hear it most in suggestions and invitations, often with ～ませんか or ～ましょうか.

Examples

You and a friend have 30 minutes before the movie.

コーヒーでも飲む？

"Want to get a coffee or something?"

Casual

A coworker looks tired after a long meeting.

お茶でも飲みませんか。

"Shall we have some tea or something?"

Polite

It's Sunday and you're both bored.

"Should we go see a movie or something?"

Casual

A guest arrives early and has to wait.

"Please read a magazine or something here [while you wait]."

Polite

With and without

Without

コーヒーを飲む？

"Do you want to drink coffee?" A question about coffee, specifically.

With でも

コーヒーでも飲む？

"Want to get a coffee or something?" Coffee is just an example. It sounds relaxed, and your friend can easily say "let's get tea instead."

Not the same as the でも that means "but". That one starts a new sentence (でも、高い). This one sits right after a noun, inside the sentence (お茶でも飲む).

N5 Grammar

～つもりだ

Polite～つもりです
Casual～つもりだ plain statement
～つもり just the word, very common

Same meaning: "plan to". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

Last Samurai Standing · Episode 1

また、刀を抜くおつもりですか？

"Are you planning to draw your sword again?"

つもり means plan to, intend to: something you've already decided to do.

It goes right after the dictionary form: 抜く + つもり. On this card, it answers "what have you made up your mind to do?": draw the sword.

Add です to make it polite. Here it's asked about someone else, so お is added on top: おつもりですか.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 14

ペン子さんにアタックするつもりで

"With the plan of making a move on Penko-san..."

Casual: つもり on its own, or つもりだ. Here it's つもりで, "with that plan in mind", and the sentence carries on.

Examples

A friend asks what you're doing this weekend. You've already booked the tickets.

土曜日に映画を見るつもり。

"I'm planning to see a movie on Saturday."

見る + つもり. Already decided, not just a wish.

Casual

Your boss asks about your plans after the contract ends.

来年、日本に引っ越すつもりです。

"I'm planning to move to Japan next year."

引っ越す + つもり + です.

Polite

Your friend thinks you'll go to the party. You won't.

今日は行かないつもり。

"I'm not planning to go today."

For "plan not to", put the verb in ない form: 行かない + つもり.

Casual

A coworker sees you packing up early.

今日は早く帰るつもりです。

"I'm planning to go home early today."

帰る + つもり + です.

Polite

With and without

Without

京都に行きたいです。

"I want to go to Kyoto." Just a wish, maybe one day.

With つもり

京都に行くつもりです。

"I'm planning to go to Kyoto." You've decided.

その ("that") + つもり ("plan, intention") + です = "that's my plan". 就職したら: "once I get a job".

結婚式出る ("go to the wedding") + つもり = "planning to go to the wedding?". こんな格好で: "dressed like this".

N5 Grammar

もらう (貰う)

YouTube · video

お水ってもらえますか?

"Could I get some water?" [to the staff at a restaurant]

もらう means to get, to receive: something comes to you from someone else.

The thing gets を (here って, casual for を), the giver gets に or から. On this card, もらえる is "can get", so もらえますか is "can I get?", the everyday way to ask for something.

Polite: もらいます, もらいました. Casual: もらう, もらった.

Examples

A coworker asks about your new watch.

父にもらいました。

"I got it from my dad."

The giver gets に: 父に. Who received? You, so no need to say it.

Polite

Your friend sees a pile of chocolate on your desk.

みんなからもらった。

"I got them from everyone."

から works too: "from everyone". に and から mean the same here.

Casual

At the hotel front desk, you want a map.

地図をもらえますか。

"Could I get a map?"

The thing gets を: 地図を.

Polite

The shop is giving away free samples.

これ、もらっていい？

"Can I take this?"

もらっていい: "is it okay if I take it?"

Casual

With and without

Without

友達が本をくれました。

"My friend gave me a book." The friend is the one doing it.

With もらう

友達に本をもらいました。

"I got a book from my friend." Same event, but told from your side: you're the one receiving.

Getting zinc from food. もらっていこう: "let's get it and go on".

もらった: I received. The giver doesn't even need to be said.

昨日、伯父さんから手紙をもらいました。

"Yesterday I got a letter from my uncle."

Giver + から this time. Same meaning as に.

キレイな石 ("pretty stones") + を + もらった ("got") = "got pretty stones". って: "she said".

お菓子 ("candy") + が + もらえる ("can get") = "you get candy". んだよ: telling the news.

N5 Grammar

あげる

YouTube · video

そして、和尚さんは、よく絵を描いて、人にあげます。

"And the monk often paints pictures and gives them to people." [a story about a temple monk]

あげる means to give: something goes away from you (or the person the story is about) to someone else.

The thing gets を, the person who receives gets に: 人にあげます, "gives to people". It never goes towards you: when someone gives something to you, that's くれる.

Polite: あげます, あげました. Casual: あげる, あげた.

Examples

A coworker asks what you did with your old bike.

弟にあげました。

"I gave it to my little brother."

The receiver gets に: 弟に. Who gave? You, so no need to say it.

Polite

Your friend admires your scarf. You don't wear it anymore.

それ、あげるよ。

"You can have it."

Literally "I'll give it (to you)". From you, to them: あげる.

Casual

It's Valentine's Day. Your friend is holding a box of chocolates.

誰にあげるの？

"Who are you giving them to?"

It also works for other people giving: here your friend gives, someone else gets.

Casual

At the park, a child asks if they can feed your dog.

犬にパンをあげないでください。

"Please don't give the dog bread."

Feeding an animal is also あげる: 犬に + パンを.

Polite

With and without

Without

友達が本をくれました。

"My friend gave me a book." The book comes to you.

With あげる

友達に本をあげました。

"I gave my friend a book." The book goes away from you, to your friend.

朱里 + に ("to") + あげる ("give") = "I'll give it to Shuri". ここ: "this place".

"I have a habit of giving away condos."

マンション ("condo") + を + あげる ("give") + 癖 ("habit") = "a habit of giving away condos".

お母さんに ("to Mom") + あげた ("gave") + 石 ("stones") = "the stones I gave Mom".

"I'll give you some flowers."

あなたに ("to you") + 花を ("flowers") + あげましょう = "I'll give you flowers", a polite offer.

"Want me to give you that?"

それを ("that") + あげよう ("let me give") + か = "shall I give you that?".

あげます ("I'll give") + よ = "you can have it". Who gets what is clear from the scene.

"Let me give you a piece of advice."

Advice can be "given" with あげる too.

N5 Grammar

くれる・てくれる

Polite

YouTube · video

今は、僕の妻のお母さんが、代わりに世話をしてくれています。

"Right now, my wife's mom is looking after [it] for us instead."

くれる means someone gives to me (or to my side: my family, my friends). After a て-form it means someone does something for me.

On this card: 世話をして + くれる. It answers "who's helping us out?": my wife's mom.

Polite: くれます. Here it's くれています, "is doing it for us" right now.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 2

じゃ、白熊君、肩揉んでくれる？

"Then, Polar Bear, will you massage my shoulders?"

Casual: plain くれる. Asked as a question, it's a friendly favor: "will you do this for me?"

Examples

Your friend just got back from Kyoto and handed you a box of sweets. You tell your sister.

友達がお土産をくれた。

"My friend gave me a souvenir."

Plain くれる: the thing comes to me. No "me" needed, くれる already says it.

Casual

A coworker likes your new pen and asks where it's from.

これ、部長がくれました。

"My boss gave me this."

Only toward you or your side. When YOU give something, it's a different verb (あげる).

Polite

You missed the bus, but your mom drove you to the station.

母が駅まで送ってくれました。

"My mom drove me to the station."

送って + くれる: she did it for me.

Polite

Your friend is about to leave, but you need one more minute.

ちょっと待ってくれる？

"Can you wait a sec?"

A question with くれる = asking a favor.

Casual

With and without

Without

友達が手伝いました。

"My friend helped." Just a fact. Helped who? Not said.

With くれる

友達が手伝ってくれました。

"My friend helped me out." It was for me, and I'm glad.

"And they even put a panda strap on it for you."

つけて + くれる: the shop does it for you.

この動画をみてくれて、ありがとうございます。

"Thank you for watching this video."

見て + くれて + ありがとう. You watched, for me.

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 4

バイト帰りに、買ってきてくれる？

"Could you buy some on your way home from work?"

A question with くれる = asking a favor.

YouTube · video

QRコードを、あの読み込んだら、そうガイドしてくれる。

"If you scan the QR code, it guides you."

Even a machine can くれる: it does something for you.

N5 Grammar

そして・それから

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 8

そして、ある吹雪の日。

"And then, one snowy day..." [telling a story]

そして means and or and then, at the start of a sentence. It hooks what comes next onto what was just said.

On this card, it moves a story along: this happened, and then, one day in a snowstorm... It answers "What happened next?".

It's the same in polite and casual speech. You hear it a lot in stories and explanations; in chat people often say それから or で.

YouTube · video

それからシャンプーとかボディーソープとか、いろんなものがあります。

"And they also have shampoo, body soap, all kinds of stuff."

それから is "and then" or "and also": the next thing in time, or the next thing on a list. Here it adds more things to the list.

Examples

Telling a friend about your morning.

朝ご飯を食べました。それから、学校に行きました。

"I had breakfast. Then I went to school."

それから = after that.

Polite

Introducing yourself.

私は学生です。そして、カフェで働いています。

"I'm a student. And I work at a café."

Polite

Telling a friend what to buy.

卵と牛乳。それから、パンも。

"Eggs and milk. Oh, and bread too."

それから adds one more thing.

Casual

Describing your hotel room.

部屋は広い。そして、すごく静か。

"The room is big. And really quiet."

Casual

With and without

Without

部屋は広いです。静かです。

"The room is big. It's quiet." Two loose facts.

With そして

部屋は広いです。そして、静かです。

"The room is big. And it's quiet." The second fact is added on.

N5 Grammar

でも

YouTube · video

めっちゃ苦い。でも、苦さが違います。

"It's really bitter. But it's a different kind of bitter."

でも means but. It doesn't attach to anything: it stands at the start of a new sentence.

On this card, the first sentence ends (苦い。), then でも turns things around: bitter, but not the bitterness you'd expect.

Works in polite and casual speech alike. Usually followed by a small pause (でも、).

Examples

A friend asks about your new apartment.

駅から遠い。でも、広いよ。

"It's far from the station. But it's big."

Casual

Your teacher asks if you did the homework.

はい、やりました。でも、家に忘れました。

"Yes, I did it. But I left it at home."

Polite

Someone says sushi is expensive in Japan.

でも、回転寿司は安いですよ。

"But conveyor-belt sushi is cheap."

The first sentence can come from the other person. でも pushes back on what they just said.

Polite

Your friend wants to go out, but you're tired.

行きたい。でも、眠い…

"I want to go. But I'm sleepy..."

Casual

With and without

Without

この店は高い。おいしい。

"This place is expensive. It's good." Two facts, no link.

With でも

この店は高い。でも、おいしい。

"This place is expensive. But it's good." Now the second sentence pushes back against the first.

Same "but" as けど and が (But), just in a different spot. けど and が glue onto the end of the first part (高いけど、おいしい). でも starts a fresh sentence (高い。でも、おいしい).

Polite

でも、このケーブルはとてもとても頭がいいケーブルです。

"But this cable is a very, very smart cable."

It looks like a plain cable, but it's not.

でも、さすがにもう穴掘りもしたいからな。

"But I really want to do some digging now too."

でもむきむきすぎないの

"But not too muscly [okay?]"

In fast casual speech the pause after でも often disappears.

Polite

Legal High · Episode 6

でも、無駄でした。

"But it was pointless."

でも ("but") + 無駄でした ("it was pointless"). でも starts a new sentence that goes against the last one.

Casual

The Journalist · Episode 6

でも狭いぞ。

"But it's small."

でも ("but") + 狭い ("small, cramped") + ぞ: rough "I'm telling you".

Polite
